title: Dharamshala march unified to honour late martyr Lobga Ranzgen
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 20:The morning air at the entrance to Tsuglakhang temple here in Dharamshala carried a mixture of mourning and charged momentum. Tibetans in dark clothes, many draped in the colours of the Tibetan national flag, hurried through the temple gates. Some walked quietly, while others moved with an unmistakable sense of urgency. The murmur of prayers can be heard along with the shuffle of hundreds of footsteps. Hundreds had come to attend a prayer service marking the 49th day since the passing of Lobga Rangzen, the Tibetan independence activist who fatally self-immolated in front of the United Nations headquarters in New York on July 2, 2026. The service was organised by the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) in collaboration with the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC). But what followed the prayers was something few had expected. As people emerged from the temple, Dharamshala witnessed a gathering of Tibetans on a scale rarely seen in recent memory. Even the crowds traditionally seen on March 10, Tibetan National Uprising Day, seemed eclipsed by the extraordinary number of people who came together that day. Such a visible and expansive representation of Tibetans had not been seen for a very long time. At around 11:40 a.m., the procession began from the temple gates, moving through the streets of Dharamshala before culminating at the Police Ground. In an unprecedented display of institutional unity in exile, the march was led by the three pillars of the Tibetan administration: the CTA President Penpa Tsering and members of his Cabinet, Tibetan Parliamentarians, and judges of the apex Tibetan court. Behind them walked Tibetans from every generation and every walk of life. Elders, a few leaning on canes, walked alongside younger demonstrators. Parents carried children as young as four or five on their shoulders. Schoolchildren from Tibetan Children’s Village in Upper Dharamshala and Gopalpur joined the procession. Families, students, monks, nuns, and ordinary residents all became part of the same moving tide—they shared one voice. Slogans calling for Tibet’s independence, voicing strong opposition to China’s so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” among other of China’s repressive policies in occupied Tibet rang through the streets, along with demands for justice for the late martyr. In his final appeal, late Lobga Rangzen had linked the absence of fundamental freedoms in Tibet to the loss of Tibetan independence, arguing that restrictions on human rights, freedom of speech, and even the display of the Dalai Lama’s portrait could ultimately be traced to that loss. His words now travelled with the procession. As the march descended into Lower Dharamshala, Indian shopkeepers and residents stepped outside their establishments, watching as the enormous procession passed before them. Former Tibetan Parliamentarian Youdon Aukatsang then urged demonstrators to raise some of their slogans in Hindi so that local residents could understand the message being carried through their streets. The chants became a bridge between the demonstrators and those watching from the roadside. Some slogans spoke directly of the universal desire for freedom and independence, while others warned against trusting China’s assurances of fraternity. Other chants accused Chinese authorities of wrongdoing. The words echoed through the lanes as the procession continued toward the Police Ground. By the time the march reached its final destination, the gathering had become more than a memorial procession. It had become a public expression of grief, political conviction, and collective identity. Speaking at the culmination of the march, Tashi Targyal, Vice President of the TYC, reiterated the message attributed to Lobga Rangzen and called on Tibetans to overcome internal divisions while remaining united in the cause of Tibetan independence. He argued that Tibetans who genuinely believe in independence should not be made to feel that their position contradicts the guidance of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. He also cautioned against portraying every political proposal or suggestion from the Dalai Lama as an instruction that all Tibetans are obliged to follow one single political path. Such interpretations, he stressed, risk creating unnecessary divisions within Tibetan society. He emphasised that the TYC regards protecting and upholding the guidance of His Holiness as a central responsibility, while also insisting that Tibetan institutions must be respected and that those entrusted with responsibilities toward the Tibetan government in exile must fulfil them with dignity. The CTA President Penpa Tsering acknowledged Lobga Rangzen’s final testament calling all Tibetans to unite and campaign for Tibet’s independence, in which the late martyr stated that his action was a protest against policies of the Chinese Communist Party and what he described as the systematic eradication of Tibetan identity in Tibet. The Tibetan political leader also highlighted the history of self-immolations by Tibetans. According to figures cited by the CTA, 157 Tibetans inside Tibet have been known to have self-immolated since 2009. Of these, 136 died, nine survived and the status of 12 remains unknown. In exile, including Lobga Rangzen, 11 Tibetans have self-immolated, nine of whom died, and two of whom survived. The CTA President’s address also turned toward what he described as the policies threatening Tibetan identity today. He highlighted concerns surrounding China’s so-called “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,” pointing to what the CTA describes as efforts to erode the Tibetan language, distort Tibetan history and identity, impose cultural assimilation at the grassroots level, Sinicise Tibetan Buddhism, intensify ethnic integration, expand technological surveillance, politically vet Tibetan cadres, undermine autonomy rights, and establish forms of extraterritorial jurisdiction. Despite the intensity of the day’s demonstrations, the CTA President reiterated that the Tibetan administration remains committed to resolving the Sino-Tibetan conflict through the Middle-Way Approach, the policy adopted by the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile. He also invoked the sacrifices of Tibetans who had died for the cause, pledging that their deaths would not be allowed to become forgotten chapters in history. For the past seven weeks since Lobga Rangzen’s death, Tibetans and supporters in different parts of the world have organised demonstrations, solidarity campaigns, prayer gatherings, and candlelight vigils to honour his ultimate sacrifice for the Tibetan cause. His death has continued to reverberate throughout Tibetan diaspora communities. The challenge now, a protester said, is whether the extraordinary fervour visible on the streets of Dharamshala can be sustained. The speeches of the leaders from across the aisle suggested that it should be. The leader of the Exile Tibetan government and that of the non -governmental organisations all echoed a common line- to ride the momentum of the global attention and churn out a sustained effort to rally support for the Tibetan cause that has received a much needed push from the sacrifice of Lobga Rangzen. The postDharamshala march unified to honour late martyr Lobga Ranzgenappeared first onPhayul.

title: Tibetan activists cycle 360 kms to Dharamshala in memory of martyr Lobga Rangzen
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 19:Braving torrential monsoon showers, scorching heat, and challenging uphill stretches, a group of ten Tibetan activists completed a gruelling cycle rally of more than 360 kilometres from Paonta Sahib to Dharamshala over six days, arriving in the hill town on Wednesday. The cyclists received a warm welcome by members of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) and the local Tibetan community upon their arrival. Soaked by the rain and visibly shivering after their arduous journey, the volunteers, dressed in black T-shirts emblazoned with the message, “Pawo Lobga Died for Free Tibet”, raised slogans calling for Tibetan independence and a free Tibet. The cyclists included TYC Paonta President Ngawang Paljor, along with Jampa Yeshi, Namgyal, Tsering Wangyal, Namgyal Tashi, Ngawang Tenpa, Tenzin Yarphel, Karma Tashi, Tsering Tenzin, and Tenzin Tsering. Organised by the Regional Tibetan Youth Congress, Paonta, the rally was held in memory of the late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, whose 49th day since passing will be observed by Tibetans worldwide tomorrow (August 20). Speaking to media representatives after reaching Dharamshala, Ngawang Paljor said the cyclists had deliberately timed their journey to coincide with the 49th-day observance. The group will participate in a joint prayer service and peaceful march organised by the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) from the Main Tibetan Temple to the Police Ground in Dharamshala. He said the campaign was also aimed at drawing greater attention to issues concerning Tibet and protesting against China’s newly implemented “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which Tibetan activists and exile leaders have criticised as another instrument of assimilation. The rally, he said, was not merely a long-distance cycling expedition but an effort to carry the Tibetan cause directly to people and the media along the route. The volunteers interacted with local communities and media organisations, including holding a press conference in Chandigarh to highlight their concerns. Reflecting on the challenges encountered during the six-day journey, he said the cyclists endured intense heat, persistent rainfall and strenuous climbs while covering approximately 40 to 50 kilometres each day. Despite the physically demanding conditions, all ten volunteers successfully completed the journey. Ngawang Paljor also expressed gratitude to India and the Indian people for their decades-long support and solidarity with Tibetans living in exile. With the 49th-day observance scheduled for Thursday, he stressed that the Tibetan community should not allow the momentum of activism to fade after the commemorative day. He urged Tibetans to continue organising campaigns and activities according to their individual capacities, saying such efforts would help preserve the message and final appeal made by the late Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who called for Tibetan independence and urged Tibetans to remain united in their struggle before setting himself on fire in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York on July 2, 2026. title: Son of Chinese activist detained over Dalai Lama photo questions “separatism” charge
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 18:The son ofimprisoned Chinese pro-democracy activist Zhang Yihas questioned the legal basis of the “inciting separatism” charge brought against his father, saying he cannot understand how the simple act of showing a photograph of the Tibetan spiritual leader, His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, could be construed as a political offence. In a testimony submitted to the New York-based human rights organisation Human Rights in China (HRIC), Zhang Hongyuan said the arrest of his father did not come as a surprise, but marked the culmination of a long-standing fear he had carried since leaving China. He now lives in the Netherlands. Zhang Yi, a retired resident of Wuhan, was detained by police in Lhasa on July 1 after showing a photograph of the Dalai Lama to a Tibetan woman at Sera Monastery. He was later placed under criminal detention and formally arrested on suspicion of “inciting separatism” under Article 103 of China’s Criminal Law. On July 18, he was transferred from administrative detention to criminal detention at the Lhasa Detention Centre. Roughly twelve days later, authorities approved his formal arrest. The charge of “inciting separatism” is based on Article 103, which criminalises actions interpreted by the state as encouraging the separation of Chinese territory. However, according to his family, Zhang Yi’s conduct bore no resemblance to political activism. Zhang Hongyuan said his father did not organise any protest, deliver political speeches, distribute material, or call for Tibetan independence. Instead, he said, his father merely showed an old photograph while attempting to communicate with a woman who did not speak Mandarin. The photo of the Dalai Lama, however, is politically sensitive in Tibet. Chinese authorities have long labelled the Dalai Lama a separatist figure, despite his attempts to seek dialogue with Beijing for genuine autonomy under the Chinese framework as prescribed in its constitution. In occupied Tibet, even possessing or displaying his photograph can be treated as a politically charged act, attracting imprisonment. Zhang Hongyuan argued that this context still does not explain the charge. “A tourist in Lhasa showed a photo of the Dalai Lama to someone who didn’t even share his language, someone who was too frightened even to look at it—and they say he incited separatism,” he said. “What did he incite? And what did he secede?” He said the central question remains unanswered: what, precisely, the authorities believe was incited in the encounter. Zhang Hongyuan said the case highlights how political meaning can be attached to even ordinary objects. In Tibet, he said, a photograph alone can be interpreted as a political act, depending on the broader framework in which it is viewed. He added that the woman at Sera Monastery appeared too fearful to engage with the image, yet the incident was still treated as serious enough to warrant criminal detention and arrest. Reflecting on the case, Zhang Hongyuan said: “Usually, it’s fathers who go to the police station to collect their sons. For me, it was a son going to the police station to collect his father.” Zhang Hongyuan has called on international observers to continue speaking about his father’s case. He said that while public attention may not immediately secure his release, it has already prompted Chinese authorities to question relatives about external reporting, indicating that scrutiny is being noticed. “I am campaigning, I am not running away, and I will absolutely not back down,” he said. title: Minnesota-Chicago ‘Peace Walk for Tibet’ in US reaches Wisconsin
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 17:The ongoing ‘Peace Walk for Free Tibet’ in the United States from St. Paul, Minnesota to Chicago reached Milton, Wisconsin on Friday where members of the local community there including Kunga Norbu, nephew of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, and Jigme Jungney, former Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s Bureau in New Delhi took part in the initiative, to show solidarity. The Peace Walk is organized by a group of Minnesota-based Tibetan activists led by Mayong Nyima and Rabga, who initiated the long-distance march to raise awareness about the situation inside Tibet and encourage Tibetans and supporters across the United States to speak up for Tibet. The initiative is among many campaigns and protests in the west as well as in the Indian subcontinent that exile Tibetans have organized following the fatal self self immolation of Tibetan activists Lobga Rangzen on July 2, 2026 in front of the UN Headquarters in New York. Organizers say his death is a painful reminder of the continuing desperation surrounding the situation in Tibet and of the responsibility of Tibetans living in free societies to ensure that the voices of Tibetans inside Tibet are not forgotten. “Now it’s time for Tibetans to stand up and voice their opinion,” Kunga Norbu said as he joined the walkers, emphasizing the importance of Tibetans living in freedom using their voices for those inside Tibet who cannot freely express themselves. A press release issued by the Wisconsin local Tibetans stated, “The participation of Kunga Norbu and Jigme Jungney in Wisconsin adds further significance to this grassroots initiative and reinforces its central message: Tibetans in the free world have both an opportunity and a responsibility to continue speaking publicly for Tibet at a time when Tibetans inside their homeland face severe restrictions on political expression”. The Peace Walk began at the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul on August 5. The marchers have since traveled through western and southern Wisconsin, reaching the Wisconsin State Capitol in Madison on August 12. The activists had already covered approximately 320 miles (514 km) since leaving St. Paul, based on the distances outlined in the route plan. The Peace Walk is scheduled to conclude in Chicago on August 19, to coincide with the 49th day following Lobga Rangzen’s death. In Tibetan Buddhist tradition, the 49th day carries profound spiritual significance and marks the completion of the traditional period of prayers and rites following a person’s death. The organizers intend the final day of the walk to serve not only as the culmination of their journey, but also as a solemn remembrance of Lobga Rangzen and his sacrifice for Tibet. The postMinnesota-Chicago ‘Peace Walk for Tibet’ in US reaches Wisconsinappeared first onPhayul.

title: Tibetan youth completes 800-km peace walk from Dharamshala to Leh for language preservation
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 17:Kalsang Tharchin, a Tibetan youth and solo marcher, reached the Tibetan settlement at Choglamsar in Leh at around 9 a.m. on Sunday, completing a month-long peace walk from Dharamshala to Ladakh to raise awareness about the urgent need to preserve the Tibetan language and cultural identity, against the threat of eradication due to China’s relentless policies inside occupied Tibet. Tharchin began his journey from Dharamshala on July 15 and walked approximately 800 kilometres across some of the Himalayas’ most challenging terrain, traversing mountain passes, valleys and remote stretches along the way. He was joined for part of the journey by Stanzin Choedak, a youth from Zanskar, who walked alongside him and supported his campaign, during the last leg of his journey. Upon reaching Choglamsar, Tharchin was welcomed by representatives of the Tibetan Settlement Office and members of the local Tibetan community, marking the culmination of a physically demanding journey undertaken to draw attention to the importance of safeguarding Tibetan linguistic and cultural heritage. Speaking to Phayul, Tharchin said the campaign was driven by concerns over policies implemented by the Chinese government that he argued threaten the survival of the Tibetan language and cultural heritage. He also said the walk was undertaken in memory of Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan independence activist who self-immolated in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York on July 2. Tharchin said his campaign was intended not merely as an expression of protest against Chinese policies, but as a positive appeal for the preservation and protection of the Tibetan language. He said the campaign also sought to draw attention to the recent implementation of China’s ethnic unity law, which he believes poses further challenges to the preservation of Tibetan linguistic and cultural identity. A white flag carried throughout the march served as the central symbol of the campaign. It bears “Ka Kha Ga Nga,” the first four letters of the Tibetan alphabet, representing the Tibetan language, along with a message conveying resilience and victory. Tharchin said the message reflects the broader purpose of the march: to defend the Tibetan language as a fundamental pillar of cultural identity and continuity. Protecting the language, he said, is itself a means of resisting policies that threaten to erode Tibetan cultural heritage. Having completed the Dharamshala–Leh leg of his journey, Tharchin said he plans to continue walking from Leh towards Pangong Tso, the high-altitude lake near the India-Tibet border, extending his campaign further into Ladakh, the Indian state that borders Tibet. title: Tibetan delegation meets UNHRC special representative, presents six demands
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 14:A Tibetan delegation, accompanied by two family members of late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, met with United Nations Human Rights Council Special Representative Anne Siyota at the United Nations on Wednesday, urging the international rights body to take more decisive action over the deteriorating human rights situation in Tibet. The delegation, led by former 13th and 14th Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) Centrex President and former Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile member Tsewang Rigzin, held discussions with Siyota for nearly an hour. Speaking toPhayulfollowing the meeting, he said the delegation submitted six demands that addressed what it described as “continuing violations”of Tibetan rights and the erosion of Tibet’s cultural and national identity. The delegation’s first demand was for the United Nations to implement its earlier resolutions on Tibet adopted in 1959, 1961 and 1965. These resolutions had raised concerns over violations of the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Tibetan people and called for an end to policies undermining their rights, including their right to self-determination. The delegation also urged the UN to dispatch an independent fact-finding mission to Tibet and recognise Tibet as an independent country, with sovereignty vested in the Tibetan people. A significant portion of the discussion focused on China’s education policies in Tibet, particularly the expansion of state-run residential boarding schools for Tibetan children. Rigzen toldPhayulthat the delegation called on the UN to exert pressure on Beijing to dismantle the boarding-school system, which they allege is designed to accelerate the assimilation of Tibetan children into Chinese society by distancing them from their families, language, and cultural traditions. The delegation further urged the United Nations to publicly oppose China’s recently implementedLaw on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, calling for the legislation to be withdrawn immediately. The sixth demand centred on what Rigzen described as the need for the United Nations to show greater solidarity with and sympathy for the Tibetan people. As part of this appeal, the delegation asked a UN representative to visit the site outside the UN Headquarters in New York where the late martyr carried out self-immolation on July 2, 2026. The Tibetan activist later died from his injuries. The delegation also called on the UN to acknowledge and honour the thousands of Tibetan men and women who, according to the delegation, have sacrificed their lives for the Tibetan cause over the years. He said the six demands were ultimately aimed at pressing the UN to move beyond expressions of concern and take more tangible steps on the Tibet issue. These, he said, should include enforcing its earlier resolutions, facilitating an independent investigation into conditions in Tibet, challenging policies viewed as threatening Tibetan identity, and giving greater recognition to the rights and grievances of the Tibetan people. The postTibetan delegation meets UNHRC special representative, presents six demandsappeared first onPhayul.

title: New visuals show intensified demolition at Larung Gar, monk detained after protest
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 14:Newly obtained photographs and video footage by Dharamshala-based media outlets showed demolition work is continuing at Larung Gar Buddhist Institute in Sertar County, eastern Tibet, offering a rare visual glimpse into the latest phase of a campaign that has already affected more than 1,000 monastic residences. The newly surfaced footage appears to show monastic residences being evicted as Chinese authorities proceed with the latest round of demolitions at one of the world’s largest centres of Tibetan Buddhist learning. According to reports, on August 9, a monk staged a protest against the demolition by displaying a large portrait of the 10th Panchen Lama from the window of a residence marked for destruction. The portrait reportedly remained suspended for a considerable period, apparently as a symbolic rejection of the authorities’ actions. The monk was subsequently detained, according to reports, and his whereabouts remain unknown. The reported detention of the monk who displayed the portrait of the 10th Panchen Lama adds another dimension to the latest demolition campaign. His current whereabouts remain unknown, highlighting concerns over the treatment of monks who publicly object to measures affecting Tibetan religious institutions. The latest demolition drive comes against the backdrop of intensified restrictions at Larung Gar, which has been subjected to successive government campaigns over the past two decades. Chinese authorities carried out major demolitions in 2001, 2016, and 2019, citing overcrowding and the lack of legally required construction permits. The latest phase began on July 13, 2026, with more than 1,000 residences reportedly slated for demolition. Founded in 1980 by the late Tibetan Buddhist master Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok, Larung Gar was established in the aftermath of the Cultural Revolution as a centre for the revival of Buddhist learning and meditation. It subsequently developed into a prominent institution for the study and practice of Tibetan Buddhism, as well as a major centre for Tibetan language and cultural education, drawing thousands of Tibetan and Han Chinese practitioners. Its rapid growth, however, brought the institute under sustained scrutiny from Chinese authorities. In 2001, authorities launched the first major demolition campaign at Larung Gar, destroying thousands of residential structures and reducing the institute’s population by roughly half. Despite continuing restrictions, the community gradually expanded again. A far larger campaign followed in 2016 and 2017 after a directive from the central government. Nearly 5,000 residences were reportedly demolished, while thousands of monks and nuns were expelled from the institute. The measures prompted international concern. In February 2017, six United Nations human rights experts warned that the actions at Larung Gar appeared to constitute “concerted attacks on tangible and intangible cultural heritage” and raised concerns over violations of the cultural rights of both present and future generations. The pressure on Larung Gar has extended beyond the physical dismantling of residences. Since 2019, Chinese authorities have progressively tightened restrictions on the enrolment and participation of Han Chinese Buddhists at the institute. In 2021, authorities reportedly introduced measures separating Chinese practitioners from Tibetan residents, further altering the demographic composition and functioning of the academy. The latest demolitions therefore represent another chapter in a prolonged process of restructuring and curbing the religious community. Access to Larung Gar has also become increasingly restricted, making independent reporting from inside the sprawling complex difficult. The emergence of the latest photographs and video footage consequently provides an uncommon glimpse into the continuing changes taking place within the institute. title: Two Tibetans honoured with ‘Rangeland Restoration Awards’ for grassroots conservation and pastoralism
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 6:Two Tibetans, Trachung Palzang from Ngawa (Ch. Sichuan) and Hashu Karma Choshas from Yushu (Ch. Qinghai), have been honoured with theRangeland Restoration Awards 2026for their contributions to grassland restoration, pastoral livelihoods, ecological conservation, and the preservation of Tibetan nomadic culture. The awards, organised under the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists (IYRP) 2026, declared by the United Nations General Assembly, recognised 20 practitioners from 90 entries across 26 countries. The awards were jointly organised by the IYRP Global Alliance and the South Asia Regional Alliance, honouring individuals whose work contributes to the restoration, sustainable management and protection of rangelands, while strengthening the pastoral communities that depend on them. Trachung Palzang, from Gascha Village in Maixi Township, Dzoge County, Ngawa Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, is described as a community-based grassland restoration practitioner and a member of a traditional herding family. According to his award profile, Palzang returned home in 2010 to address grassland degradation and help safeguard pastoral culture. He subsequently combined traditional pastoral knowledge with modern ecological approaches and, in 2013, founded a grassland restoration cooperative, alongside a herder photography group that has engaged hundreds of pastoralists in ecological restoration and cultural preservation. His work has reportedly contributed to the restoration of approximately 14,000 mu, or 933 hectares, of degraded alpine grasslands and peat wetlands through community-led approaches. Palzang has also promoted summer enclosure and winter grazing, as well as adaptive grazing practices aimed at improving the sustainability of rangeland management. His initiatives have benefited about 280 pastoral households, representing more than 1,200 people, while engaging over 1,000 herders. His conservation efforts have also focused on biodiversity, with his award profile noting improved habitat conditions supporting 98,000 sheep units and more than 230 wildlife species. Beyond ecological restoration, Palzang has worked to strengthen indigenous knowledge and pastoral culture, including through the establishment of a herder photography group and a community conservation model that has reportedly been replicated by more than 10 organisations. Hashu Karma Choshas, from Jialo Grassland in Drido County, Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, is recognised as a nomadic educator, cultural heritage bearer, and grassland guardian. A member of a pastoral community, he founded the Polar Nomadic School, an initiative that integrates ecological education with traditional nomadic knowledge. The school has reportedly reached more than 5,000 students, herders, and teachers. His work extends beyond environmental conservation to the preservation of Tibetan nomadic heritage. He is recognised as a county-level intangible cultural heritage bearer for Shengto-style black-tent craftsmanship and has worked to revive and preserve the traditional craft. He has also founded the Yushu Third Pole Ecological Nomadic Culture Protection and Development Research Service Center, linking cultural preservation with community-based ecological conservation. His award profile credits him with protecting and restoring more than 5,000 mu, approximately 333 hectares, of alpine grassland through rotational grazing. The landscape lies near the source of Drichu (Yangtze River) and the headwaters of the Neqü River and supports approximately 300 yaks and 100 Tibetan sheep within a traditional pastoral setting. He has additionally worked with local communities to conserve water sources, particularly the headwaters of the Neqü River, while promoting ecological education and traditional pastoral knowledge. The recognition comes at a time when Tibetan pastoral communities face mounting pressures from environmental degradation and policies by the Chinese government that have disrupted their traditional relationship with the land. Large-scale infrastructure under the pretext of development projects—including roads, airports, dams, mining operations, reservoirs, solar power facilities, and national parks—have transformed vast stretches of traditional grazing grounds, while other interventions have further restricted access to pasturelands. Under the Chinese government’s ecological and animal husbandry policies, nomads have increasingly been restricted from seasonal grazing and, in many areas, compelled to settle in fixed locations. Grasslands have been fenced off, converted for other uses, or subjected to large-scale mining and other development activities, contributing to ecological degradation and the fragmentation of traditional pastoral landscapes. These changes have had consequences beyond the environment. The displacement of nomadic communities and restrictions on traditional pastoral practices have disrupted longstanding livelihoods, weakened community networks, and placed pressure on the transmission of Tibetan language, culture, and pastoral knowledge. The postTwo Tibetans honoured with ‘Rangeland Restoration Awards’ for grassroots conservation and pastoralismappeared first onPhayul.

title: Flash floods, debris damage roads, pastures at sacred Mount Amnye Machen
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 7:Flash floods and extensive debris flows struck Mount Amnye Machen in Machen County, Golog Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Amdo (Ch. Qinghai), on the evening of August 5, damaging roads and bridges and burying large stretches of pastureland, following what a source in exile described as a glacier collapse on the mountain. The source in exile who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons toldPhayulthat the glacier collapse triggered torrents of water, mud, and rock that swept through an uninhabited section of the mountain. No human or livestock casualties have been reported, but the debris flow has covered substantial areas of surrounding pasture under thick layers of mud and debris. The source said the scale of the flooding and debris flow has significantly altered parts of the landscape and warned that unstable terrain could continue to pose risks to pilgrims travelling along the mountain’s traditional circumambulation route. Chinese authorities, however, attributed the damage to heavy rainfall and mudslides. An official notice dated August 25 stated that rural roads and bridges had been damaged and warned of geological hazards and risks to traffic safety. Authorities subsequently prohibited vehicles and pedestrians from entering the affected areas, citing the need to safeguard lives and property. The notice did not mention a glacier collapse. The disaster has also disrupted a major pilgrimage season at Mount Amnye Machen, one of Tibet’s four principal sacred mountains. The mountain holds particular religious significance during the Year of the Horse, when large numbers of Tibetan pilgrims traditionally undertake the circumambulation around its sacred perimeter. Following the flooding, authorities suspended pilgrim travel along the affected routes. Despite indications from local officials that repairs would be completed swiftly, the roads remained closed as of September 6. Many pilgrims have consequently been stranded in the Tamchok Gongkha area of Yaekhok village, waiting for the route to reopen so they can resume and complete their pilgrimage. Warnings circulating on Tibetan social media have urged pilgrims to exercise caution, citing the continuing possibility of avalanches, landslides and other hazards along sections of the circuit. The flooding has also renewed longstanding concerns among local Tibetans over the environmental impact of mining in the Amnye Machen range. According to the exile source, discussions circulating on Tibetan social media have linked the recent glacier collapse and flooding to decades of mining activity around the mountain, although the connection has not been independently established. Local residents have reportedly observed a marked retreat of glaciers in recent years, exposing ground and animal trails that were previously covered by thick layers of ice. The changes have fuelled concerns about the mountain’s increasingly fragile environment and the potential risks facing communities and pilgrims who depend on the surrounding landscape. Mining operations in the Amnye Machen range reportedly began around 1993, with operations transferred to Qinghai West Copper Co., Ltd. in 1997. Over the following decades, intensive mineral extraction, particularly for copper, has drawn repeated criticism from local residents and Tibetan environmental advocates over its alleged impact on the ecology of the sacred mountain range. Concerns have also been raised over alleged pollution of the Guchu River. Local accounts have claimed that untreated industrial wastewater was discharged directly into the river, rendering the water unsuitable for consumption by nomadic communities and contributing to livestock deaths. Residents have repeatedly appealed to local authorities over the alleged environmental damage associated with mining. On August 21, 2017, they reportedly submitted a petition to Chinese central government departments calling for the mining project to be halted. According to local accounts, however, their appeals have not resulted in a substantive halt to mining activities. The latest disaster has consequently intensified concerns over the deteriorating ecological conditions around Mount Amnye Machen, where glacial retreat, extreme weather, mining activity and the seasonal influx of pilgrims converge in a landscape considered sacred by Tibetans. title: China restrict Tibetan volunteers, relief efforts in flood-hit Kyirong
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 4:Chinese authorities have imposed stringent restrictions on movement into flood-hit Kyirong region in occupied Tibet, preventing Tibetans from other parts of the region from travelling to the disaster zone to provide relief and express solidarity with affected communities, according to an exile-based source who spoke to Phayul on condition of anonymity for safety reasons. The source said the Chinese government has adopted an unusually restrictive approach to relief efforts in Kyirong, where severe flooding has affected areas along the Tibet-Nepal border. “Many Tibetans want to travel to Kyirong to help the affected people, but they are not being allowed to enter the area,” the source told Phayul, adding that the restrictions appear particularly stringent given the region’s proximity to Nepal. According to a government notice issued following the floods, entry into the affected border area is restricted to officially designated relief personnel. Civilians and personal vehicles are prohibited from entering the disaster zone, while travel from Saga, Tingri and Nyalam Counties into Kyirong has been explicitly barred for civilians. Authorities have warned that those who violate the restrictions could face severe legal consequences. The source contrasted the restrictions with the response to the devastating January 2025 Dingri earthquake, during which some Tibetan-led relief and assistance efforts were reportedly permitted. “This time, the restrictions are much stricter. During the 2025 Dingri earthquake, some Tibetans were able to provide assistance, but in Kyirong they are not allowing such efforts at all,” the source said. The source stated that the heightened controls may be linked to Kyirong’s strategic location on the Nepal border, where authorities are particularly sensitive to the movement of people and information. Meanwhile, Chinese state controlled propaganda mouthpiece have released carefully curated photographs and videos showing government-led rescue and relief operations in the affected areas. The imagery focuses on state-organised emergency responses and relief personnel, while independent access to the disaster zone remains heavily restricted. In the aftermath of the catastrophic floods and mudslides that swept parts of the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, Chinese authorities reported 31 deaths and 531 people missing in occupied Tibet as of September 4. The figures, however, remain impossible to independently verify, as journalists, international humanitarian organisations, and other independent observers continue to be denied access to the disaster-affected areas. The absence of independent access has compounded concerns over the transparency of the official casualty figures and left substantial gaps in public knowledge about the scale of the devastation. For families searching for missing relatives, the restrictions have created an acute information vacuum, prolonging an agonising wait for credible and timely confirmation of their loved ones’ fate and whereabouts. Chinese authorities said that, by noon on September 2, they had received 876 calls reporting people dead or missing—448 from within China and 428 from overseas. The volume of calls highlights the magnitude of the uncertainty surrounding the disaster and the growing demand from families for reliable information from authorities. The postChina restrict Tibetan volunteers, relief efforts in flood-hit Kyirongappeared first onPhayul.

title: Dalai Lama returns to Dharamshala after more than two-month sojourn in Ladakh
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 4:The Tibetan spiritual leader His Holiness the Dalai Lama returned to Dharamshala on Friday after spending more than two months in Leh, Ladakh, bringing to a close an extended summer sojourn marked by religious teachings, public audiences, and engagements with people from across the Himalayan region. The nonagenarian leader was warmly welcomed by thousands of Tibetans and local Indian residents who lined the streets of Dharamshala as his convoy made its way to his residence. The spiritual leader had been in Ladakh from June 28 to September 4, following medical treatment for his left knee in Delhi. His annual summer visits to Ladakh have become a longstanding practice, allowing him to escape Dharamshala’s intense monsoon season while continuing his religious and public engagements in the Himalayan region. During his stay, the Dalai Lama held public audiences in Leh for 49 days, receiving a total of 21,572 people. He also attended a Long-Life Prayer offering at the Kalachakra Teaching Ground, a gathering that reflected the region’s distinctive interfaith character. The prayer ceremony was jointly organised by the Ladakh Buddhist Association, Ladakh Gonpa Association, the Muslim communities represented by Anjuman Imamia and Anjuman Moin-ul-Islam, and the Christian community of Ladakh. The Dalai Lama’s return to Dharamshala follows a period of heightened attention to his health and mobility. He underwent surgery on his left knee in June this year in Delhi, following a successful right knee replacement performed in June 2025 at Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) in New York, one of the world’s leading orthopaedic centres. After his 2025 procedure, the Tibetan spiritual leader spent a period recovering in Syracuse, New York, where he underwent extensive physical therapy before returning to Dharamshala. Despite persistent mobility challenges, the Dalai Lama has maintained a demanding public schedule in recent years, continuing to conduct religious teachings, grant audiences, and participate in official and community engagements. During large public gatherings, he has occasionally relied on aides and a golf cart to cover longer distances between his residence and the Tsuglagkhang, the Main Tibetan Temple, where he regularly conducts teachings and public ceremonies. title: Real Madrid deletes Nepal-Tibet flood post after Chinese backlash
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 3:Spanish football powerhouse Real Madrid has deleted a social media post referring to victims of the devastating Tibet-Nepal floods, days after the club came under intense criticism from Chinese state media and online users for using the word “Tibet” rather than Beijing’s sinicised term “Xizang.” The post, which had appeared on Real Madrid’s official social media platforms on August 30, featured a photograph of players observing a minute’s silence at the Santiago Bernabéu for victims of the catastrophic floods and landslides that struck communities on both sides of the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26. The accompanying message referred to those affected in “Nepal and Tibet.” The post was removed on September 3, following mounting criticism in China. Although Real Madrid has not publicly stated that the deletion was made in response to Chinese pressure, its removal came after Chinese state-affiliated media and online users repeatedly demanded that the club retract or amend the wording. The Global Times, a Chinese Communist Party mouthpiece, urged Real Madrid to replace “Tibet” with “China’s Xizang”, arguing that the club’s humanitarian gesture had been overshadowed by what it described as politically inaccurate wording. The newspaper stressed that “Xizang is an inalienable part of China” and said placing it alongside the sovereign nation of Nepal ran counter to the one-China principle. Chinese social media users also piled pressure on the club, calling for the post to be deleted and for Real Madrid to issue an apology. The criticism was accompanied by a pointed reminder of the club’s commercial stakes in the Chinese market. The Global Times noted that Real Madrid commands a sizeable following in China and has cultivated long-term commercial interests across Asia, warning that the club’s public communications are therefore expected to meet a higher threshold of sensitivity when addressing territorial issues. The deletion marks a striking turn in a controversy that began with what was ostensibly a humanitarian gesture. A football club’s expression of solidarity with victims of a natural disaster has instead become entangled in one of China’s most sensitive political fault lines: the terminology used to describe Tibet. Beijing officially refers to Tibet as “Xizang” and has increasingly sought to promote that terminology in international discourse. The Chinese government regards Tibet as an integral part of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and strongly objects to language that, in its view, treats Tibet as a separate political entity. Real Madrid’s decision to remove the post, without publicly explaining the reason, has therefore raised questions over the extent to which China’s political sensitivities can shape the public communications of major international brands seeking to maintain relations with Chinese audiences. The episode also illustrates how the language surrounding Tibet has become a contested arena far beyond diplomatic and political circles. Even a condolence message from one of the world’s most prominent football clubs has been subjected to scrutiny over whether it conforms to Beijing’s preferred nomenclature. The dispute comes as the humanitarian toll from the August 26 disaster continues to mount. A massive ice-and-rock avalanche near the Tibet-Nepal border unleashed catastrophic flash floods, devastating communities and infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing. As of September 3, Nepal had recorded at least 1,252 deaths, while more than 4,200 people remained missing. Across the border in occupied Tibet, Chinese authorities have officially acknowledged 16 deaths and hundreds of people missing, even as Kyirong—one of the hardest-hit areas—bore the brunt of the devastating floods. The stark disparity in reported casualties has fuelled concerns over the transparency and completeness of information coming from the Tibetan side of the border.
