title: Tibetan, Chinese pro-democracy advocates adopt joint declaration at Dharamshala forum
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 3:A three-day forum bringing together Tibetan and Chinese scholars, policy experts, and human rights activists concluded in Dharamshala on Wednesday with a joint call for nonviolence, democratic reform, and sustained dialogue as pathways towards a peaceful resolution of the Tibet-China conflict. The “Democratic China and Future of Tibet Forum”, organised by the Tibetan Community Development Fund (TCDF) in collaboration with the Central Tibetan Administration’s official think tank, Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), brought together 29 participants from India, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Australia, Japan, Taiwan, and Southern Mongolia. Convened to foster candid exchanges on democracy, human rights, and Tibet’s political future, the forum sought to bridge perspectives between Tibetans and Chinese pro-democracy activists and explore avenues for greater cooperation between the Tibetan and Chinese democratic movements. The forum opened on August 31 with a keynote address by CTA President Penpa Tsering, who spoke on Sino-Tibetan relations, the Middle Way Approach, the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama, and the importance of cooperation between Tibetans and Chinese. The discussions culminated in five declarations covering nonviolence, a shared democratic future, Tibetan democracy and history, the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation, and the legal and human-rights implications of China’sLaw on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress. The first declaration established nonviolence as a common guiding principle for addressing the Tibet-China conflict. Participants drew on the longstanding advocacy of the 14th Dalai Lama and Chinese democracy advocate Liu Xiaobo, emphasising peaceful resistance, dialogue, and pragmatic engagement as alternatives to confrontation. The second declaration called for a shared vision of a democratic future, urging closer interaction between Tibetans in exile and Chinese democracy organisations and individuals. Participants also highlighted the value of sharing the Tibetan exile community’s experience of democratic governance as part of broader efforts towards democratisation in China. Discussions under the third declaration focused on Tibet’s history, Tibetan-Chinese exchanges, Tibetan democracy, and the Middle Way Approach. Participants said greater understanding of Tibetan perspectives among Chinese audiences, alongside deeper Tibetan engagement with China’s democracy movement, could help build trust and create space for meaningful dialogue. The declaration also called for greater efforts to explain the Middle Way Approach to Chinese people. The policy, advocated by the Tibetan leadership in exile, seeks genuine autonomy for Tibetans within the framework of the Chinese Constitution rather than outright independence. The fourth declaration addressed the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama, rejecting any role for the Chinese government in the process. Participants stated that the authority to determine the Dalai Lama’s succession rests with the Dalai Lama and the Dalai Lama’s private office, Gaden Phodrang Trust, in accordance with Tibetan Buddhist traditions. The fifth declaration raised concerns over China’s so-called “Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress,” calling for its immediate repeal. Participants argued that the legislation could have far-reaching consequences for the linguistic, cultural, religious, and national identities of Tibetans, Uyghurs, Southern Mongolians, and other ethnic communities. The participants said the forum marked a step towards establishing a sustained platform for Tibetan-Chinese academic and policy engagement, with continued communication and cooperation envisioned as a means of building mutual understanding and strengthening nonviolent approaches to the long-running conflict. The postTibetan, Chinese pro-democracy advocates adopt joint declaration at Dharamshala forumappeared first onPhayul.

title: Book honouring Lobga Rangzen’s legacy launched in Dharamshala
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 2:Marking two months since the passing of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, a collection of 77 essays and prose pieces written by Tibetans in the aftermath of his self-immolation was launched on Wednesday at the Tibetan Settlement Office (TSO) hall in Dharamshala. The volume brings together writings that appeared across social media platforms following Lobga Rangzen’s death, documenting the reflections, emotions, and political sentiments expressed by Tibetans in his memory. Lobga Rangzen self-immolated on July 2, 2026, outside the UN headquarters in New York. In his message, the late martyr strongly condemned China’s repressive policies in occupied Tibet and its ongoing campaign to assimilate and ultimately erase the Tibetan people. He called on fellow Tibetans that restoration of Tibet’s independence is the only lasting solution to end the sufferings endured under China’s colonial occupation. Speaking about the motivation behind compiling the book, Loyak Tashi, who compiled the collection, said the idea emerged within a week of Lobga Rangzen’s passing. During that period, he noticed a growing number of essays and prose pieces being written and circulated online in remembrance of the activist. He said Tsering Logye, the editor of the book, approached him and suggested bringing the writings together in a single volume. The conversation prompted him to undertake the compilation, as he feared that many of the tributes and reflections would gradually disappear from public memory within a year or two. He said the book was therefore intended not only to preserve those writings but also to honour what he described as Lobga Rangzen’s “ultimate sacrifice.” Among the speakers at the launch was Dr Sonam Tobgyal, a researcher at Tibet Watch and an advocate for Tibetan independence, who said he had read most of the pieces in the collection after encountering them on social media. Reflecting on the writings, he said he sensed a renewed expression of support for the Tibetan independence cause among those who had written them. He contrasted this with the situation roughly 15 years ago, when, in his assessment, relatively few Tibetans were paying sustained attention to the independence movement. While acknowledging that activism around Tibetan independence had continued, he said the past decade had been particularly difficult for advocates of the cause. According to his observation, many activists within the Tibetan community have faced challenges while organising campaigns and advocating for independence at both individual and organisational levels. He further noted what he described as a growing distance among some Tibetans from the broader Tibetan cause, particularly at times when international governments offered limited support or when the situation inside Tibet deteriorated. However, he said Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation appeared to have rekindled a sense of urgency and responsibility among sections of the Tibetan community. He said the act had reminded people of the importance of keeping the Tibetan issue alive and continuing efforts on behalf of Tibet. He also pointed to what he described as a renewed engagement among younger Tibetans, saying that a strong sense of commitment to the independence cause had been largely absent among younger generations for some time. According to him, young Tibetans have often grown up hearing that achieving independence from China is extremely difficult, that China is too powerful, and that Tibetans could benefit by remaining within China. He said discussions about collectively working toward Tibetan independence had consequently received less emphasis in their upbringing and education. He argued that Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation had helped revive those sentiments across different sections of Tibetan society, with its impact being felt among both younger and older generations. Another speaker at the launch was Rangzen Dhondup, a close friend of the late activist and president of the Dharamshala regional chapter of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC). He said he had known Lobga Rangzen for nearly a decade through their shared involvement in the Tibetan cause. Recalling the day of Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation, Rangzen Dhondup said the late martyr had called him at around 10 a.m. IST. At the time, he was attending the annual general meeting of the TYC in Poanta Sahib and was unable to take the call. He instead sent him a message explaining that he was in a meeting and would call him later. He said he could never have imagined that the missed call would come only hours before Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire. He learnt of the self-immolation from a friend early the following morning and said he initially struggled to believe what had happened. He recalled that Lobga Rangzen had served two consecutive terms with the Tibetan Youth Congress’ New York and New Jersey chapter beginning in 2017, before later becoming involved with the Tibetan National Congress (TNC). Rangzen Dhondup said the two remained in regular contact, frequently discussing campaigns, sharing updates on activities and exchanging ideas on advancing the Tibetan cause. According to him, Lobga Rangzen also consistently supported campaigns organised by the TYC Dharamshala regional chapter, including through financial contributions. He described him as a person deeply committed to preserving Tibetan identity and consistently advocating campaigns in support of Tibetan independence. The postBook honouring Lobga Rangzen’s legacy launched in Dharamshalaappeared first onPhayul.

title: CTA reaffirms democratic legacy on 66th Tibetan Democracy Day
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 2:The exile Tibetan government, officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), on Wednesday commemorated the 66th anniversary of Tibetan Democracy Day at the Tsuglagkhang Temple in Dharamshala, reaffirming the democratic institutions established under the visionary leadership of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. The commemoration brought together representatives of the three pillars of the Tibetan democratic system—the CTA President Penpa Tsering and members of his Cabinet, elected members of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, and judges of the Tibetan Supreme Justice Commission—along with members of the Tibetan community and 30 Chinese pro-democracy activists. Among the Chinese activists was Dang Yang, a veteran of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests who was subsequently imprisoned twice by the Chinese Communist government. Addressing the gathering, the Tibetan political leader condemned China’s newly implemented Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which came into effect on July 1, warning that the legislation and accompanying policies warrant a firm and appropriate response. “These include severe restrictions on the Tibetan language; the falsification of history and identity; forced cultural assimilation at the grassroots level; the Sinicisation of Tibetan Buddhism; enforced ethnic integration; pervasive technological surveillance; political and social coercion; the political vetting of Tibetan cadres; the violation of regional autonomy rights; and the assertion of extraterritorial jurisdiction targeting organisations and individuals worldwide,” the Tibetan leader said. He said the Chinese Communist government’s policies since its colonial occupation of Tibet have consistently sought to undermine Tibetan identity, particularly through restrictions on language, religion, and culture. Urging Tibetans both inside Tibet and in exile to make the preservation of their heritage part of everyday life, he called for greater participation in institutional initiatives to safeguard the Tibetan language and cultural identity. “On our part, it is not enough merely to declare opposition and protest; we must expose and confront these malicious policies based on a well-informed understanding. We therefore urge all Tibetans to join the Central Tibetan Administration in these vital efforts,” he stated. Dang Yang, speaking at the commemoration, described the Tibetan democratic system as a model of democratic resilience and said its experience offered important lessons to China’s pro-democracy movement. “The Tibetan experience has demonstrated to the world that even without a territory under its actual control, without an army, a democratic system can still function successfully and generate powerful political influence,” Dang said. He contrasted the Tibetan exile administration’s democratic legitimacy with what he described as the Chinese Communist Party’s reliance on “violence, lies, and control.” “The Tibetan community in exile, by contrast, relies on the recognition of its people, democratic legitimacy, and the cohesion of its institutions,” he said. Dang sated that the Tibetan democratic system has helped unite Tibetans dispersed across the world and ensured the continuity of their political voice across generations. “It is precisely this democratic system that has brought together Tibetans scattered across the world, generation after generation. It has ensured that the Tibetan voice has not been silenced by the Chinese Communist Party, and that the Party has never been able to represent the Tibetans or determine their future,” he said. Dang also announced plans for the establishment of a China Congress, a proposed democratic representative institution outside the framework of the Chinese Communist Party. He said the initiative has not yet been formally established but has already attracted more than 1,000 founding electors. “We hope to begin a democratic practice belonging to the Chinese people outside the system of the Chinese Communist Party, and to accumulate experience about China’s future democratic transition and constitutional development,” he said. He said China’s democracy movement could draw particularly from the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile’s experience of electoral representation. “The Tibetan experience of election has enabled representatives with a mandate from the electorate to continue making their voices heard in the international community,” Dang said, adding that China’s democracy movement has yet to develop a representative institution with a comparable electoral foundation. Looking ahead to a possible democratic transition in China, Dang said a future Chinese political system must abandon coercive policies towards Tibetans and instead respect their cultural, religious and national identity. “A future democratic China must never again treat Tibetans through oppression or forced assimilation. Instead, it must respect the Tibetan people’s culture, religion, language, national identity, and fundamental rights,” he said. He called for future relations between the Chinese and Tibetan peoples to be founded on equality and peaceful dialogue rather than political domination. Dang further proposed establishing a sustained platform for dialogue between Tibetans and Han Chinese living overseas, covering political and cultural questions related to Tibet as well as the future spiritual and cultural relationship between the two peoples. He concluded by expressing hope that Tibetans and Chinese alike would eventually be free from authoritarian rule and able to determine their own futures. The Tibetan democratic system began taking shape soon after the Dalai Lama arrived in India in exile. The process formally began with the establishment of the Commission of Tibetan People’s Deputies in 1960, followed by the drafting of constitutional frameworks in 1961 and their promulgation in 1963. A major milestone came in 1991 with the adoption of the Charter of Tibetans-in-Exile, which established a democratic system founded on the separation of powers and independent institutions. In 2001, Tibetans began directly electing the head of the Kashag, or Cabinet. A decade later, in 2011, the Dalai Lama devolved his remaining political and administrative authority and transferred it fully to democratically elected Tibetan leaders. The postCTA reaffirms democratic legacy on 66th Tibetan Democracy Dayappeared first onPhayul.

title: Tibetan researchers, activists demand transparency from China over Kyirong flash floods
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 1:A joint press briefing in Dharamshala on Tuesday raised alarm over what activists and researchers described as an ‘information blackout’ surrounding the devastating flash floods in Kyirong in occupied Tibet, demanding that China release full and verifiable information on casualties, missing persons, displacement, destruction, and its emergency response. The briefing, titled “Asia’s Water Tower in Crisis: Tibet-Nepal Flash Floods Demand Transparency,” was organised by the International Tibet Network (ITN) and Students for a Free Tibet–India (SFT-India) at the Tibetan Settlement Office (TSO) hall in Dharamshala. The briefing brought together researchers, activists, and a Tibetan monk from Kyirong, including Dhondup Wangmo, Research Fellow at the Environment and Development Desk of the Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), the Central Tibetan Administration’s think tank; Dr Lobsang Yangtso, Senior Environmental Researcher at ITN; Jampa Palden, a monk from Kyirong; and Tashi Dhondup, Campaigns Coordinator at SFT-India. The speakers called on Beijing to provide complete, accurate, and timely information about the scale of the disaster, warning that withholding, manipulating, or selectively releasing information could endanger communities both within occupied Tibet and downstream in Nepal and India. Jampa Palden, who is from Kyirong, shared accounts received from family members in the region, claiming that the entire Lhende area had been severely inundated and that three villages along the Lhende River had been completely washed away. According to his account, each of the three villages was home to at least 30–40 households. He added semi-nomadic Tibetan communities predominantly inhabit the area and is also an important trade corridor linking Tibet with Nepal. Chinese state-controlled media have so far reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing. The discrepancy between limited official reporting and accounts emerging from outside Tibet was cited at the briefing as evidence of the urgent need for independent access and transparent reporting from the disaster zone. Dr Lobsang Yangtso said that while the precise causes and trajectory of the recent glacial outburst have not yet been scientifically established, the disaster should prompt scrutiny of the rapid expansion of infrastructure across the environmentally fragile Himalayan region. She argued that extensive construction of roads, bridges, and hydropower projects in high-risk areas could compound the effects of climate-driven hazards, including glacial lake outburst floods, ice and snow avalanches, and other forms of cryospheric instability. She also pointed to the accelerating effects of climate change on the Tibetan Plateau, describing Tibet as an exceptionally climate-sensitive region. According to figures cited at the briefing, the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan region contain around 63,000 glaciers, 25,000 glacial lakes, 766 identified glacial-lake flood hazards, and 716 ice- and snow-avalanche hazards. “These risks,” she warned, could pose serious threats to communities in the future, particularly as warming alters the stability of glaciers and high-altitude landscapes. She also drew attention to China’s ongoing construction of a proposed 60-gigawatt hydropower project in Medog County, Nyingtri Prefecture, Tibet, close to India’s Arunachal Pradesh border. She warned that large-scale infrastructure development in such an ecologically sensitive and climate-vulnerable landscape could have ramifications far beyond Tibet and across downstream areas, including India, Nepal, and Bangladesh. The speaker therefore called for an international moratorium on mega-development projects in Tibet, arguing that large projects should not proceed until Tibetans can freely provide or withhold their consent without fear of detention, intimidation, or other forms of repression. She further urged Himalayan countries to consider an immediate moratorium on large hydropower projects until comprehensive climate, environmental and disaster-risk assessments are completed. The briefing also scrutinised the role of multilateral development banks and international financial institutions in financing hydropower projects across the Himalayas. Lobsang Yagntso specifically raised concerns over international financing for the Trishuli River hydropower project in Nepal, arguing that financial institutions must be held accountable when projects proceed despite known glacier-related risks and insufficient environmental assessment. She pointed to the vulnerability of hydropower infrastructure to sudden glacier-related disasters and questioned whether lenders have adequately incorporated increasingly volatile climate and geological conditions into their risk assessments. She argued that financial institutions should not treat Himalayan hydropower projects solely as development or investment opportunities while overlooking their potential consequences for workers, local communities, and downstream populations. The briefing called for independent monitoring, real-time data sharing, and effective cross-border early-warning systems, including timely notification of dangerous glacier movements, glacial lake outbursts, sudden rises in river levels, and other foreseeable hazards. The speakers called on China to grant unhindered access to affected Tibetan areas to international humanitarian organisations, independent journalists, disaster-response agencies, and human rights monitors. They also urged Beijing to ensure that Tibetans who document the disaster or communicate information about the humanitarian situation are not subjected to surveillance, detention, intimidation, prosecution, or other reprisals. The briefing also appealed to international governments, media organisations, humanitarian agencies, and monitoring bodies to use Tibetan place names consistently in official statements, reporting, and documentation. The organisers argued that accurate Tibetan terminology is not merely a linguistic preference but a matter of factual accuracy, cultural respect, and recognition of Tibetan identity. They urged international actors to avoid uncritically adopting Chinese state terminology, including “Xizang,” particularly when reporting on humanitarian, environmental, and human rights issues. The postTibetan researchers, activists demand transparency from China over Kyirong flash floodsappeared first onPhayul.

title: China censors Kyirong flood footage, grossly under-reports death toll
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 31: Video footage capturing the terrifying moments when people fled a rapidly advancing wall of mud and debris at the Kyirong Port in occupied Tibet has reportedly been removed from Chinese social-media platforms, fuelling concerns over Beijing’s censorship of information surrounding the devastating Himalayan floods. The footage, which circulated online following the disaster, reportedly shows people scrambling to escape moments before torrents of mud and floodwater engulfed parts of the Kyirong Port. Copies of some of the videos have continued to circulate outside China after the original posts were reportedly deleted. Kyirong County, a strategically important trading gateway between occupied Tibet and Nepal, was among the worst-affected areas on the Tibetan side. The Kyirong Port, a major land crossing, suffered severe damage; roads, buildings, and infrastructure were inundated or swept away. As of Monday, Chinese authorities have reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in Kyirong County, according to reports citing official figures. By comparison, the death toll on the Nepalese side had risen to 903, with 4,247 people still missing. The stark disparity is particularly striking given that Kyirong was among the areas hardest hit by the catastrophic floods. The figures have intensified scrutiny of the disaster and raised questions about the true scale of casualties in occupied Tibet, where access for independent journalists and observers remains severely restricted. Reports by Indian and international media outlets have stated in their reports that several videos documenting the disaster disappeared from Chinese social-media platforms. Some reports also allege that accounts posting information about casualties and the devastation were removed or restricted. Chinese authorities, however, have rejected allegations that they are suppressing information about the disaster. Authorities have also taken administrative action against people accused of spreading what they described as rumours concerning casualty figures and the scale of the disaster. The reported removal of eyewitness footage is significant because access to Tibet for foreign journalists and independent observers remains highly restricted. In such circumstances, videos recorded by residents, workers, and travellers can provide rare visual evidence of events unfolding in the region. The disappearance of footage has therefore added another layer of controversy to an already catastrophic disaster, particularly as official casualty figures continue to evolve while hundreds remain unaccounted for. Meanwhile, Chinese state media coverage of the disaster has largely centred on rescue and relief operations, repeatedly showcasing images of emergency personnel searching through debris, evacuating residents, and delivering supplies. While such footage documents the ongoing response, the emphasis on rescue efforts, rather than the full extent of the destruction and human toll, has been criticised as presenting a sanitised picture of the catastrophe and potentially obscuring the severity of the disaster on the Tibetan side. The contrast between official coverage and eyewitness footage circulating outside China has further fuelled concerns about information control and the suppression of independent accounts. With hundreds of people still unaccounted for in Kyirong, observers say, the disappearance of videos and restrictions on information could make it increasingly difficult to establish the disaster’s full human cost. The postChina censors Kyirong flood footage, grossly under-reports death tollappeared first onPhayul.

title: New visuals show China pressing ahead with demolitions at Tibetan Buddhist institute of Larung Gar
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Recent photographic evidence and satellite imagery show Chinese authorities are continuing their latest round of demolitions of monastic residences at the Serthar Larung Five Sciences Buddhist Academy, popularly known as Larung Gar, in Serthar (Chinese: Seda), Kardze (Ganzi) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan province in eastern Tibet. The International Campaign for Tibet (ICT)first reportedthe new demolition drive launched by authorities on July 13 at Larung Gar, one of the world’s largest Tibetan Buddhist academies. Images and video taken on August 13 and satellite images — from July 27, obtained by ICT and from August 14, obtained by Radio Free Asia (RFA) — reveal the systematic destruction of monastic residences at Larung Gar. ICT Research found that the physical destruction of monastic residences at Larung Gar is occurring alongside a sustained ideological campaign to “Sinicize” Tibetan Buddhism and erode Tibetan religious and cultural identity, while imposing a state-mandated national identity centered on loyalty to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Combined with sustained political indoctrination, these demolitions disrupt collective study and practice at Larung Gar and undermine the academy’s capacity to operate as an autonomous center of Tibetan Buddhist learning. “The destruction at Larung Gar is not simply the demolition of buildings; it is part of a wider systematic campaign to bring Tibetan Buddhism under the control of the CCP,” said Tencho Gyatso, President, International Campaign for Tibet. “By demolishing the residences that sustain collective Buddhist study while subjecting monastics to relentless political indoctrination, the Chinese government is attacking both the physical foundations of religious life and the Tibetan beliefs, identity, and community they support.” “ICT calls on the international community to intervene urgently by pressing for an immediate halt to the demolitions, independent access to Larung Gar and protection for its monastics and residents. ICT also urges global leaders to raise Larung Gar directly with Chinese authorities and hold them accountable for violations of religious freedom and Tibetan cultural rights,” Gyatso added. The August 13 photographs show demolition crews targeting monastic residences, while high-resolution satellite imagery from July 27 shows that the demolitions were concentrated around the center of the academy. The August 14 imagery obtained by RFA shows a demolished area around the center, with the curved road leading to the central structures cleared — further evidence that the demolitions continued after July 27. Sources told ICT that the current phase of demolitions was scheduled to conclude by August 20. ICT is concerned that another phase may follow, as the authorities’ stated target was the demolition of at least 1,060 residences. Despite intensified surveillance and restrictions on communications and movements, ICT will continue to monitor developments at Larung Gar. The following photographs of Larung Gar emerged a month after the demolitions began. Collectively, these images provide visual confirmation of large-scale, mechanized demolition involving multiple excavators and work crews. They show that the demolitions took place during both daytime and nighttime and affected residential areas in the center of the academy. An August 13-dated photograph shows Chinese authorities continuing their latest round of demolitions at Larung Gar, a month after they began on July 13, 2026. (ICT sources) One daytime photograph shows the demolition activity amid densely packed red monastic residences that are characteristic of Larung Gar. Multiple excavators stand on a slope amid large piles of rubble and debris from destroyed buildings. Workers wearing red hard hats and high-visibility yellow vests can be seen standing along a yellow-railed pathway and among the ruins. Another August 13-dated photograph shows proximity of the latest round of demolition work being carried out at Larung Gar to the center of the Buddhist academy. (ICT sources) Another photograph taken at night shows a large SANY excavator operating under bright lights on a steep, rubble-strewn incline amid piles of broken concrete, bricks, and other debris. In the background, a large structure with illuminated golden roofs, most likely the main assembly hall at the center of the academy, remains standing, highlighting the proximity of the demolition work to the center of the complex. A photograph showing the latest round of demolition of monastic residences at Larung Gar. (ICT sources) Another photograph shows a Zoomlion excavator high on a hillside, dismantling structures or clearing debris. Green safety netting covers part of a nearby building. In the foreground, a bilingual banner in Chinese and Tibetan reads “Forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation”. The background reveals the extensive spread of Larung Gar’s red wooden huts across the valley and hillsides, underscoring that the demolitions are taking place within the heart of the monastic complex. High-resolution satellite imagery from July 27 obtained by ICT shows that the demolitions are concentrated around the center of Serthar Academy. When compared with freely available Google Earth imagery from August 10, 2019, significant changes are visible around the academy’s central area. Later imagery from August 14, obtained by Radio Free Asia (RFA), shows a cleared area around the center, with the curved road leading to the central structures cleared and dump trucks and excavators visible. Overall, the satellite imagery and the photographs together confirm that Chinese authorities are continuing this latest round of demolitions at Serthar Buddhist Academy, which ICT first reported on July 17. Planet Labs satellite imagery of Larung Gar on July 27, obtained by ICT. Planet Labs satellite imagery of Larung Gar on August 14, obtained by RFA. Google Earth imagery of Larung Gar on August 10, 2019. These demolitions are occurring against the backdrop of the Chinese government’s new so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which took effect on July 1, 2026, and longstanding policies emphasizing the “Sinicization” of Tibetan Buddhism and its subjugation under the leadership of the CCP. Earlier demolition campaigns in 2001 and 2016 similarly involved work teams accompanied by security personnel, homes marked for destruction, residents forced to sign documents agreeing not to return, and monastics bused away from the academy. The cumulative impact of these successive rounds of demolition campaigns has been a substantial reduction in the physical footprint and population of Serthar Academy, transforming parts of what was once a densely inhabited religious valley that accommodated around 40,000 practitioners at its height. The current demolitions at Serthar Larung Gar are not merely administrative or logistical measures; they are a physical expression of a repressive Chinese state policy aimed at forging “a sense of Chinese national community” and ensuring the “Sinicization of religion.” The visual evidence documents the ongoing physical destruction, but these changes are inextricably linked to a parallel ideological campaign designed to transform the academy from an autonomous center of Buddhist learning into a tightly managed institution aligned with CCP priorities. The Chinese state’s physical intervention is driven by mandates requiring monastics to prioritize political reliability over traditional Buddhist study. This is framed through the Chinese party-state’s concept of the “sense of community for the Chinese nation,” a directive explicitly delivered to senior religious leaders. During a January 2022“tea reception”for Tibetan New Year celebrations, religious leaders — including Khenpo Tsultrim Lodro, the academy’s executive vice dean and Khenpo Sodargye, executive deputy director of its management committee — were instructed by Party officials to deepen the “Sinicization of religion” and play an active role in safeguarding national unity. Such public rituals serve a specific purpose: to enlist prominent Tibetan Buddhist figures to legitimize state policies. By demanding pledges of loyalty and broadcasting their compliance on state television, the authorities aim to project an image of harmony while reinforcing a strict hierarchy of subordination. Serthar Larung Gar’s two Khenpos were required to attend the then-Kardze (Ganzi) prefecture party secretary Shen Yang’s New Year “tea reception” in 2022. (State media Kardze TV broadcast screenshot, Jan. 2022) The physical dismantling of Larung Gar has consistently been preceded by political indoctrination, often referred to by the Chinese state as “patriotic re-education.” These sessions are designed to instill absolute loyalty to the Chinese state and the CCP. A key component of this indoctrination is the affirmation of the “five identifications,” which require monks and nuns to identify with “the great motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the CCP and socialism with Chinese characteristics,” as represented in thisMay 2021 reporton activities in the academy. This ideological framework seeks to ensure that the monastic community functions as a subset of the broader Chinese national identity rather than as part of a distinct Tibetan cultural or religious entity. Political indoctrination session at Serthar Buddhist Academy where monastics were required to affirm the “five identifications”. (State media handout, May 2021) In January 2026, the state-controlled Serthar County Buddhist Association intensified this campaign by launching adrivefocused on the “Three Consciousnesses”; national consciousness, citizen consciousness, and rule-of-law consciousness. Its primary goal is to force monastics to internalize the principle that “national law is greater than religious rules.” By embedding this hierarchy into the daily life of the academy, the state aims to align the thoughts and actions of religious practitioners with the decisions of central and provincial Party committees. A political meeting convened by the state-controlled Serthar County Buddhist Association in session. (State media handout, January 2026) Chinese authorities’ push to forge a national community is also framed as central to national security. Inmid April 2026, the academy was subjected to a series of “National Security Education” activities, including mandatory flag-raising ceremonies and oath-taking events. These sessions are designed to cultivate a “collective sense of responsibility” among both monks and cadres to ensure the state’s security. This campaign has also reached deep into monastics’ private lives through “outreach activities” that bring legal and political propaganda directly into their living quarters. By distributing handbooks on national security and anti-espionage laws, the state attempts to cultivate support for its Chinese national security agenda and effectively turn the monastic community into a monitored and self-monitoring unit of the state. Officials speaking about national security to a group of Serthar monks on China’s National Security Education Day. The red banner in Chinese reads “Serthar Larung Gar Buddhist Academy’s National Security Day Publicity Meeting, April 15”. (State media handout, April 2026) The physical demolitions of monastic residences and the sustained ideological indoctrination sessions are taking place in parallel at Larung Gar. The destruction of residential housing systematically dismantles the physical infrastructure that sustained it as an autonomous religious center, dispersing its community, disrupting collective monastic life, and making it far more difficult for the academy to function as an independent hub of Buddhist learning and practice. At the same time, the indoctrination sessions work to replace traditional religious identity with a state-mandated national identity, requiring monastics and residents to internalize party ideology, loyalty to the Chinese state, and a redefined sense of belonging that prioritizes political allegiance over spiritual lineage and Tibetan cultural identity. By forcing Larung Gar to “adapt” to a socialist society, the Chinese government is not merely changing an institution but is systematically eroding its autonomy. Material destruction and ideological indoctrination work together to significantly restrict the academy’s ability to operate according to its own religious and communal traditions. Instead, it is being reshaped to serve the singular goal of a unified, “sinicized” national community in which independent centers of Tibetan Buddhist authority are subordinated to state and Chinese Communist Party control. The postNew visuals show China pressing ahead with demolitions at Tibetan Buddhist institute of Larung Garappeared first onInternational Campaign for Tibet.

title: Family, lawyers of imprisoned Tibetan businessman denied visits, as authorities censor renewed calls for justice online
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Despite guarantees under China’s Prisons Law, Chinese authorities have repeatedly denied requests by lawyers of imprisoned Tibetan businessman Dorjee Tashi (Duoji Zhaxi) to visit him, including requests made as recently as July-August, according to an August 12, 2026-dated post on Chinese social media describing lawyers’ failed attempts to arrange such visits. Authorities have also been censoring information about the denial of Tashi’s visitation rights and have sought to silence any advocacy online on his behalf. Once a successful businessman and philanthropist in Tibet, Dorjee was first arrested in 2008, amid the wide-scale protests in Tibet that year, for allegedly “funding activities that endanger national security.” He is currently serving a life sentence in Lhasa’s Drapchi Prison, formally known as the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) Prison number 1, on politically motivated charges of “loan fraud.” In August 2021, ICT published Dorjee’stestimonydetailing the torture he suffered during his pre-trial detention. Advocacy by Chinese rights advocates, legal observers, and family members on behalf of Tashi on Chinese social media continues to be censored by authorities, ICT found. Shortly after an August 1 post argued that Tashi’s life imprisonment constitutes a “profound miscarriage of justice,” Chinese censors removed the post. It was reposted on August 12, but authorities took it down again shortly afterwards. The latest suppression of online advocacy on behalf of Dorjee Tashi has left the family, lawyers, and supporters even more frustrated with the Chinese legal system, as it follows years of authorities thwarting his family’s activism through sit-ins and lawyers’ challenges to his wrongful imprisonment and efforts to secure a retrial. When the previously taken-down August 1 post was reposted on August 12 on Chinese social media platform WeChat, the International Campaign for Tibet archived the page. The original WeChat link now displays a message in Chinese stating: “This content cannot be viewed due to violations. Following related complaints, this content violates the ‘Cybersecurity Law of the People’s Republic of China’”. The post’s repeated removal highlights the authorities’ persistent efforts to silence online discussion of the case after dismissing years of grassroots advocacy that called for due process and a retrial. Dorjee Tashi before his imprisonment in 2008. Tashi’s supporters lamented in the August 12 social media post that authorities had refused to grant a retrial, despite repeated appeals by family members and lawyers over ten years. This, they add, reflects authorities’ politically motivated violation of the legitimate rights and interests of prisoners and their families, as provided under China’s Prisons Law, and is not a case of the defense lacking evidence for a retrial. Supporters argue that the “loan fraud” conviction that Tashi was charged with has no real basis. They note that Tashi’s company had put up assets worth about 16.09 million yuan as collateral for a 1.5-million-yuan bank loan and that the principal and interest were repaid in full by 2013. They argue it was a civil loan dispute, not criminal fraud, as there was no intent to cheat the bank and the collateral far exceeded the loan. In addition to the broader legal issues surrounding his case, Tashi’s family and lawyers face severe restrictions on prison visits. In the initial years after his sentence began, family visits were allowed, but prison authorities began to limit the visits starting in 2019, without citing any clear legal reason. Dorjee Tashi’s elder brother and eldest sister have not seen him since their last visit in 2019 and his second sister since 2021. His wife and children have been denied visits for about two years since 2024. Defense lawyers Liu Zheng and Wang Fei have repeatedly submitted formal requests to meet Tashi but have faced delays, refusals, additional conditions or “retaliatory law enforcement” for exercising their right to demand justice through online channels. According to a social media post citing the lawyers, prison authorities denied lawyer Wang Fei his request to visit Tashi because he had informed the family that Tashi reported being beaten in prison during their last meeting which took place inOctober 2025, as reported by ICT. Prison officials also reportedly demanded that the family delete online posts about the case and issue an apology before authorities would consider allowing any visits. Tashi’s supporters say this turns a legal right into a bargaining chip and punishes people for speaking out. They demand that the TAR prison immediately stop linking visitation rights to online speech and allow the family and lawyers to visit. The supporters also urged prison officials, prosecutors, and disciplinary bodies to investigate the repeated denial of visits over the years and hold accountable those responsible. With Tashi having spent about 18 years in prison under a life sentence on spurious and politically motivated charges, his supporters have made renewed calls for a full retrial and the return of basic visitation rights that Chinese authorities have denied him for far too long, in clear violation of China’s own laws. The postFamily, lawyers of imprisoned Tibetan businessman denied visits, as authorities censor renewed calls for justice onlineappeared first onInternational Campaign for Tibet.

title: Ahead of crucial 21st Party Congress, China cultivating a more repressive leadership in Tibet
author: International Campaign for Tibet
content: Seventh-generation leadership in Tibet will be shaped by two guiding principles that institutionalize centralized Party control and accelerate Beijing’s forced assimilation of Tibetans: the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law and Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building. The International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) released its 2026 Tibet Leadership Report, an annual report on the status of governance of Tibet, in which it states that Beijing is cultivating a more repressive leadership in Tibet, ahead of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) pivotal 21st Party Congress in 2027. Through leadership appointments, new legislation, and Party directives, China is deepening political control over Tibet and accelerating its policies of forced assimilation of Tibetans, amid a continued lack of any meaningful Tibetan representation in senior leadership positions, ICT said. The report finds that the “Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” and “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building” together form the legal and ideological foundations of a new governance model that prioritizes political loyalty, centralized Party authority, national security, and implementation of assimilation policies over meaningful Tibetan representation. Rather than replacing existing policies, these developments institutionalize them, embedding assimilation into the governance of education, language, religion, culture, and ethnic affairs. The report argues that the Ethnic Unity Law is Beijing’s most significant legal codification of assimilation policies to date, expanding Party authority over education, language, religion and culture while accelerating the shift toward Mandarin-medium education and restricting space for Tibetan identity. While leadership changes are expected across China and Tibet in 2026–2027, the report concludes that these changes are more likely to reinforce than alter existing policy. Drawing on new leadership data, the report finds that Tibetans remain largely excluded from positions of real political authority, with meaningful decision-making continuing to rest overwhelmingly in the hands of non-Tibetan Party leaders. As of July 31, 2026, Tibetans hold only 62 of 240 (25.8%) senior leadership positions across provincial, prefectural, and county levels, while non-Tibetans occupy 178 (74.2%). The absence of Tibetans is most pronounced in the Party, security, military, and judicial institutions that exercise the greatest political authority. The CCP’s 21st Party Congress in 2027 is expected to be a defining political moment for Xi Jinping’s next phase of leadership. Whether Xi Jinping chooses to elevate a potential successor or further consolidate his personal authority, the Congress will shape China’s senior leadership and policy direction for the next five years. The report argues that the leadership transition surrounding the 21st Party Congress is not simply about personnel changes, but about institutionalizing a new model of governance in Tibet. As leadership, ideology, and law become increasingly intertwined, Tibet offers an early indication of Xi Jinping’s governing vision for the post-2027 era – one that will guide the anticipated new seventh generation leadership of Tibet and have implications for the rights, identity and future of the Tibetan people.
