They further called on the UN and the UN Human Rights Council to take a stand on the case of Lobga Rangzen and to address the critical situation in Tibet. Upon their arrival in Dharamsala, the Tibetan Youth Congress held a press conference on August 19, 2026, at the site of the TYC hunger strike front of the Tibetan Market, near the Dalai Lama’s temple in McLeod Ganj, Dharamsala, H.P, India. Ngawang Paljor, President of the Paonta Sahib Regional Tibetan Youth Congress, said: “There are ten cyclists and eight support staff, for a total of 18 Tibetans. The goal of our bike ride is to raise awareness among the general public and Indians in particular about the Tibetan cause. We also held a press conference in Chandigarh and distributed leaflets about the Pawo Lobga Rangzen and the critical situation in Tibet.” When asked what challenges they had faced along the way, he replied, “We didn’t run into any major problems; the sun and the heat were the hardest things to endure during the bike ride. Some of us got sick, but we still managed to reach our destination (Dharamshala).” The President said, “We have three demands. First, we call on the UN and international organisations to hold the Chinese government accountable for implementing repressive policies in Tibet, particularly the “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”, as well as for the serious human rights violations committed in the region, including detentions, arrests, acts of torture, and the imprisonment of Tibetans who are merely exercising their fundamental rights to protect their language, their environment, and their faith in their spiritual leaders, notably His Holiness the Dalai Lama. Second, we condemn and reject the so-called ‘Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.’ Third, we thank the Indian government and people for hosting Tibetans for more than 70 years.” Tibet Human Rights China UNO

title: China and India hold key border issue talks ahead of expected President Xi visit to India
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug25’26) – India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi have on Aug 25 held the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the India-Tibet boundary question in Beijing ahead of an expected visit to India next month by President Xi Jinping for the BRICS Summit. The talks focused on the boundary question, bilateral relations and regional and international developments, as New Delhi and Beijing seek to consolidate a cautious stabilisation in ties following the prolonged military stand-off in eastern Ladakh triggered by the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, said indiatoday.in Aug 25. The report said the meeting assumed added significance as it took place ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on Sep 12 and 13, which is expected to see participation by Chinese President Xi Jinping, although Beijing has not officially confirmed his visit yet. The visit, should it take place, will be Xi’s first in seven years. A potential meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Xi on the sidelines of the summit could provide political momentum to efforts to improve bilateral relations. The two last met in Aug 2025 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin, the report said. The two sides have plenty of issues, including weighty ones, to discuss on their differences as well as scopes for cooperation. To India, one of the most important issues is the situation along its border with Chinese occupied Tibet on which there has been no progress at all on a settlement. Discussions still continue to be focused on maintaining the peace even as the two sides continue to sustain their build-up and remain battle-ready at all times. India has repeatedly maintained that peace and tranquillity along the border are fundamental to the wider relationship. Speaking at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum in New Delhi on Aug 22, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar reiterated that peace and tranquillity in the border areas were a prerequisite for stable relations between the two countries, the report said. NSA Shri Ajit Doval co-chaired the 25th Meeting of SRs on India-China Boundary Question with his counterpart H. E. Wang Yi, Member of the Politburo of the Central Committee of the CPC and China’s Foreign Minister on 25 August 2026 in Beijing. (Photo courtesy: X/India in China) It also cited India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) as describing developments along the border as a matter of the “most serious” concern. Its spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, also said recently that maintaining peace and tranquillity along the LAC was of “utmost importance”, stressing that the situation on the frontier would determine the overall trajectory of India-China relations. China, however, continues to give less importance to the border issue, and more on other areas of bilateral ties between the two sides, including especially trade and investment on which it already enjoys huge and growing advantages. The trade balance has continued to balloon in China’s favour despite India’s constant efforts, year after year, to get Beijing to address the increasingly unsustainable imbalance by opening up its markets to Indian products and services. On the border issue, while the disengagement process in eastern Ladakh has helped ease some of the immediate military tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the broader boundary dispute remains unresolved. Arunachal Pradesh continues to be one of the most sensitive components of the dispute, the report noted. China has enhanced its claims on the entire Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which it has taken to refer to as “Zangnan”, or southern Tibet, in recent years. India has consistently rejected the claim, maintaining that the state is an integral and inalienable part of itself. The India-Tibet boundary extends approximately 3,488 km and remains disputed across three broad sectors, with significant differences between the two sides over their respective perceptions of the LAC. While a final settlement still remains a far cry, the two sides have worked out a structured channel for senior-level political communication, particularly during periods when tensions along the frontier have threatened to spill over into the wider relationship. Ahead of the Doval-Wang meeting, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian described the Special Representatives talks as the “main channel” for negotiations between China and India on the boundary question and an important platform for communication on issues of mutual interest. The Aug 25 talks mark the latest high-level diplomatic engagement as both sides seek to maintain that current stabilisation while differences over the boundary remain unresolved, the report said. The Doval-Wang talks could help provide a diplomatic backdrop for high-level engagement between Modi and Xi by addressing sensitive areas of disagreement and reinforcing existing understandings on maintaining peace along the LAC, the report added.

title: China is building a vast ‘national ring road’ uniting the entire PRC borderlands
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug24’26) – China is building a vast “national ring road”, known as the “border-coast loop”, meant to be a national unity road in the wake of the recent implementation of its national Ethnic Unity Law, encompassing the borders of the entire current territories constituting parts of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). China has outlined plans to build a massive road-link snaking along the PRC’s land borders and coastlines – an ambitious project that could boost incomes in a string of remote regions, but also provoke geopolitical and ecological risks, reported the scmp.com Aug 23. It said the project is framed as an effort to boost economic development, social stability and national unity, with its more than 25,000km (15,500-mile) route set to run through several regions with large ethnic-minority populations – including Tibet and the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region (East Turkestan). Like the numerous other gargantuan projects China has carried out over the years or is still carrying out, the “border-coast loop” also has to overcome many challenges. Beijing will need to navigate some tricky geopolitical terrain to complete the road, which will run close to areas subject to territorial disputes, while also managing ecological hazards in rugged landscapes with fragile ecosystems, the report noted. One part of the road project – dubbed the “golden border-coast loop” by Chinese state media – is due to be completed by 2030 and will be made up of three sections, the report said, citing a five-year blueprint issued by China’s Ministry of Transport in July. The first section – the G219 highway – runs through the PRC’s southwest and far west, from Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region through Yunnan province and Tibet autonomous region to the northernmost tip of Xinjiang. Stretching 10,000km, the route will closely follow the PRC’s borders with Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, India, Bhutan, Nepal, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Russia, the report said. “This entire transport loop will not only offer the public a fresh road trip experience, but will also unlock tremendous benefits in industrial synergy, border consolidation and border-area stability and development,” the Ministry of Transport was quoted as saying. Beautiful yet remote areas in Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia that had long been inaccessible for most tourists would now become easily reachable, it has added. The report said the project also appeared to dovetail with Beijing’s new ethnic unity law, which came into effect in July and signals a shift in policy towards assimilation. * * * But Beijing is likely to run into challenges as it pushes forward with construction. For one thing, the thaw in relations between China and India remains shaky after years of border disputes that at times spilled over into deadly confrontations. India views the G219 highway with concern. In 2024, New Delhi protested the road upgrades and extensions taking place in disputed border areas – part of the preparatory work for the G219 project – which it framed as an attempt by China to alter the facts on the ground in the region, the report noted. Environmental protection is stated to be another concern. In June, a report by China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment on its key projects for the next five years noted that several areas near the road would require continuous monitoring, including the alpine border regions of Tibet, desert areas in southern Xinjiang, and Tianshan mountains’ glacial regions, the report noted. But despite these challenges, China’s connectivity push is stated to go far beyond the loop project. The country has already built the world’s largest highway and rail networks, which increasingly extend into Tibet and Xinjiang. In August, Beijing established the Xinjiang-Tibet Railway Company to oversee the construction of a 1,980km line running from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa to Hotan in Xinjiang, the report noted. Earlier, in 2022, China unveiled plans for a new highway between Lhunze in southern Tibet and Mazha in Xinjiang, which will also run near areas subject to overlapping claims from Beijing and New Delhi. The road, which will intersect with the G219, is currently under construction, the report said.

title: US envoy concludes Ladakh visit, misses Dalai Lama meeting
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug23’26) – A strongly anticipated meeting between the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, and Tibet’s exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, in the Union Territory of Ladakh did not take place after all. The Dalai Lama has been sojourning in Ladakh since Jun 28 for an extended summer stay while Gor arrived there on Aug 20 after high-profile engagements in neighbouring Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). Gor’s visit was the first by a top US envoy to this strategic frontier region of India since the 2020 Galwan clashes and subsequent border standoff with China. While in J&K, Gor, speaking to reporters alongside Chief Minister Omar Abdullah following their high-level dialogue, remarked, “Kashmir is an important part of India. I am visiting the place for the first time. It is an incredibly beautiful place.” Gor concluded his visit to J&K and Ladakh on Aug 21, after visiting the centuries-old, 12-storeyed Thiksey Monastery, one of the largest and most prominent monasteries in central Ladakh, located about 19km from capital Leh. The monastery is widely noted for its resemblance to the Potala Palace in Tibet’s capital Lhasa. The monastery’s top lama, Thiksey Rinpoche, has regularly welcomed the Dalai Lama during his annual summer visits to Ladakh over the past many years. Gor showed keen interest in Ladakh’s spiritual heritage and cultural traditions. He spent about half an hour visiting the temples and learning about Ladakh’s tradition, Buddhist heritage and more about the place, reported the f reepressjournal.in Aug 22. One of the main attractions there is the Maitreya Temple, which commemorates the visit of the 14th Dalai Lama to this monastery in 1970. It features a 15-metre (49 ft) high statue of Maitreya, the immediate future Buddha, which is the largest such statue in Ladakh, covering two stories of the building., the report noted. Still, the most telling event of Gor’s first trip to Ladakh was a meeting that never took place, said indiatoday.in Aug 21. The Central Tibetan Administration of the exile Tibetans told the media that there was a change in the programme on the night preceding Gor’s visit, and so the meeting did not happen. But neither side has explained why. And in diplomacy, that silence usually says more than a statement would, the report said. At least one comment on X said the decision smacked of pressure from China: “ China ka danda pada lagta hai, ” noted the news outlet FirstPost on its on X account Aug 20. * * * Indeed, the decision may have to do with the fact that Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit the United States in the next two weeks, as revealed by President Donald Trump while addressing a Republican campaign rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on Aug 21, according to a mid-day.com report Aug 22. Trump did not provide a specific date, venue or agenda for his expected meeting with Xi, the report said. Also, a meeting between the US ambassador and the Dalai Lama, whom Beijing regards as a separatist threat to its rule over Tibet, and that too on Ladakhi soil, would have been read in Beijing as Washington needling China on its most sensitive frontier. Besides, it was something better avoided ahead of a BRICS Summit being hosted by India next month, said the indiatoday.in report. The Kashmir and Ladakh legs of Gor’s trip form one story: an envoy with real proximity to the Oval Office, moving through India’s frontier geographies, saying just enough to please New Delhi, and doing just enough to avoid antagonising Beijing, the report concluded.

title: Report: Tibet repression intensifying as Xi looks to prolong his rule beyond 21st Party Congress in 2027
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug22’26) – China is cultivating a more repressive leadership in Tibet as it has begun implementing its forced assimilation policy there under the cover of its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress (Ethnic Unity Law), and ahead of the pivotal 21 st Congress of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in 2027. As a result, the seventh-generation leadership in Tibet will be shaped by two guiding principles that institutionalize centralized Party control and accelerate Beijing’s forced assimilation of Tibetans – the Ethnic Unity Law and Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building – said Washington-based International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) as it released its 2026 Tibet Leadership Report on Aug 18. Citing leadership appointments, the new legislation, and Party directives, the group says China is deepening political control over Tibet and accelerating its policies of forced assimilation of Tibetans amid a continued lack of any meaningful Tibetan representation in senior leadership positions. The group notes that the Ethnic Unity Law is Beijing’s most significant legal codification of assimilation policies to date, expanding Party authority over education, language, religion and culture while accelerating the shift toward Mandarin-medium education and restricting space for Tibetan identity. Drawing on new leadership data, the report finds that Tibetans remain largely excluded from positions of real political authority, with meaningful decision-making continuing to rest overwhelmingly in the hands of Chinese Party leaders. “As of July 31, 2026, Tibetans hold only 62 of 240 (25.8%) senior leadership positions across provincial, prefectural, and county levels, while non-Tibetans occupy 178 (74.2%). The absence of Tibetans is most pronounced in the Party, security, military, and judicial institutions that exercise the greatest political authority.” Referring to the absence of Tibetans in the higher echelons of the CCP leadership, the report refers to the fact that in the powerful United Front Work Department (UFWD), which oversees Beijing’s Tibet policy, there has not been a Tibetan at the senior leadership level since Sithar (Si Ta) retired as Vice Minister in 2016. In this scenario, the Ethnic Unity Law further weakens the protections nominally guaranteed under China’s regional ethnic autonomy system. Its implementation is expected to accelerate President Xi’s assimilation move and leave future Tibetan leaders with little scope to uphold the autonomous rights guaranteed under the Constitution and the Law on Regional Ethnic Autonomy, the report says. The report says currently, the highest CCP leadership positions in the Tibetan areas are held by non-Tibetans, and there is no indication that Tibetans will assume leadership positions in the coming years. The report notes that in the current, 20th Party Congress, Yan Jinhai (born 1962), former Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) Chairman and current Chair of the TAR People’s Congress, is the only Tibetan in the CCP Central Committee. Karma Tseten (Chinese: Gama Cedain, born 1967), Phurbu Dhondup (Pubu Dunzhu, born 1972), and Tsering Thar (Cering Tar, born 1969) are the only three ethnic Tibetans in the 171 alternate members of the 20th Party Central Committee. (Based on savetibet.org report Aug 18, 2026)

title: Australian Senator urges targeted sanctions on Chinese leaders enforcing transnational Ethnic Unity Law
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug22’26) – An Australian Senator has on Aug 20 called for targeted sanctions against Chinese leaders responsible for carrying out transnational repression against Tibetans and others under Beijing’s recently enforced Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress. This law on forced assimilation of Tibetans and other ethnic minority groups in the People’s Republic of China includes provision to punish those, whether within or outside the country, who oppose or criticize its implementation. In his remarks in the Australian Senate, Senator Dean Smith raised concerns about China’s new “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” and its potential impact on Tibetans living in Australia, said a Tibet.net report Aug 21. Smith, who is the Co-Chair of the Australian Parliamentary Group for Tibet, has said that Australia is home to vibrant Tibetan, Uyghur, Hong Kong and other diaspora communities who come to this country seeking freedom, democracy and the protection of the rule of law. They should never have to fear that exercising those freedoms in Australia could place them or their families overseas at risk. He has expressed alarm that for members of the Australian Tibetan community, simply voting in elections for the Tibetan government in exile, publicly supporting the Dalai Lama, or expressing their cultural and religious identity could potentially be interpreted by Chinese authorities as conduct falling within these sweeping laws. He has therefore called on the Australian Government to recognise transnational repression as a genuine national security threat and to consider targeted sanctions, including Magnitsky-style sanctions, against individuals responsible for organising or directing overseas repression and intimidation. The Magnitsky sanctions programme is a targeted US government initiative used to freeze assets and ban travel for foreign individuals and entities responsible for human rights abuses or major corruption. Named after Russian lawyer Sergei Magnitsky, the framework, initially passed by the Congress in 2012 to target Russia but expanded globally in 2016, provides for penalizing wrongdoers without targeting entire countries. Magnitsky was a Russian tax lawyer who died in a Moscow prison in 2009 after he uncovered a massive, $230 million government corruption scheme.

title: Prayers, protests mark 49th day of Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation death, and to protest China’s forced assimilation move in Tibet
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug21’26) – Prayer services as well as peace and protest marches have been held by Tibetan communities and supporters across the free world Over Aug 19-20, marking the end of the seven weeks since Lobsang Palden, better known by his independence-activist name Lobga Rangzen, carried out his protest self-immolation in front of the UN Headquarters in New York city and succumbed to his injuries on Jul 2. The events highlighted China’s current move to forcibly assimilate the Tibetan and other “ethnic minority” peoples through its recently implemented Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which Lobga Rangzen had highlighted in his last message, with a call for Tibetan unity to fight for independence. The 49 th day is significant in the Tibetan Buddhist funerary service as the day by which a deceased person is believed to have left their intermediate state for their rebirth. Enlightened beings are believed to determine their own rebirth, although China has sought to upend this by requiring reincarnation of Tibetan Buddhist leaders to be determined only by its atheist leaders’ choices, opening every possibility for making of wrong choices. In Dharamshala, the exile Tibetan headquarters, the Kashag (cabinet) of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), and the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile jointly organized a prayer service in the Tsuglakhang, the main Buddhist temple in the area, followed by a peace march from there to the downtown Police Ground, both of which reportedly saw participation by over 5,000 Tibetans. Top exile Tibetan leaders led both those events. The CTA leadership led a 49th‑Day Prayer Ceremony and a Peaceful March in Dharamshala to honour Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen. (Photo courtesy: Tibetan Parliamen-in-Exile) On the same day, the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC), which campaigns for Tibet’s independence, concluded a 33-day relay hunger-strike near the gate of the Tsuglakhang, with the campaign action scheduled to be continued in front of the UN Headquarters in New york City from the following day. The day also saw a Regional TYC group, with 13 participants, from the Tibetan settlement in Poanta Sahib conclude a 360-km bicycle rally in honour of and to pay tribute to Lobga Rangzen for his ultimate sacrifice. The rally was given a rousing reception. The Kashag was also stated to have dispatched instructions to all Tibetan Settlement Offices and Offices of Tibet to organise similar prayer services in their respective regions, ensuring that Tibetans across the world could collectively remember and honour those who had made the ultimate sacrifice for Tibet. Protests were also held in several Indian cities, including New Delhi, Kolkata, Dharamshala, Chennai and Bengaluru, among other centres, with many of the events being addressed by Indian leaders and supporters. * * * “Today marks the 49th day since he passed away. It is the final prayer for him and a day to reaffirm our struggle for freedom against China,” chosun.com Aug 20 quoted a Tibetan attending the “Lobga Rangzen 49th-Day Memorial Service” in New York City as saying. The report cited organizers as saying nearly 1,000 Tibetans from across North America, including New York, New Jersey, Canada, and Europe, had visited the site of Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation. Colourful flowers and hundreds of candles surrounded an altar set up at the site, with Tibetan monks in maroon robes seated behind them. The low chanting of Buddhist scriptures echoed through Manhattan’s city centre. Above their heads, the Tibetan snow lion flag fluttered in the wind alongside the US flag, the report noted. It said participants sat on the ground, listening to the monks’ prayers or holding placards reading “FREE TIBET.” Next to the memorial space, large banners displayed images of Rangzen engulfed in flames alongside slogans: “UN, Do Not Turn Away,” “Lobga Rangzen’s Last Wish,” and “Freedom for Tibet, China Out.” “We hope the international community, including the UN, will support the Tibetan people’s struggle for freedom,” the report quoted a participant handing out leaflets as saying. On Aug 19, family members of Lobga Rangzen, joined by TYC leaders, met with the US Special Coordinator for Tibetan Issues Riley Barnes “to brief the US government on his sacrifice, his final message, and the circumstances surrounding his death.” The meeting provided an opportunity for Lobga’s family to share their concerns and to urge continued US attention to the human rights situation in Tibet and the issues that motivated his final act, the ANI report Aug 20 cited them as saying. * * * In the Swiss city of Geneva, which hosts the UN Human Rights Council headed by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, more than 1,000 Tibetans and supporters from across Europe commemorate the occasion on Aug 19. The event featured a large-scale prayer gathering and demonstration, which began with a march from the Palais Wilson to the United Nations Office, culminating near the Broken Chair, a longstanding symbol of opposition to landmines and violence. Later in the evening, the participants gathered at the same location to hold a candlelight prayer ceremony in remembrance of Lobga Rangzen and his sacrifice, said the office of Tibet, Geneva, in a Tibet.net report Aug 21. The report said the commemoration brought together Tibetan communities and organisations from Switzerland and Liechtenstein, Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, France, Austria, Sweden, Italy and the United Kingdom, alongside the Swiss Tibetan Women’s Association, the Gesellschaft Schweizerisch-Tibetische Freundschaft (GSTF), the Tibetan Youth Association in Europe (TYAE), and V-TAG. Tibetan community leaders from across Europe have addressed the gathering. Others who gave addresses were stated to include Cédric Jeanneret, Member of the Grand Council of Geneva (the parliament and law-making body for the Republic and Canton of Geneva), and Merce, Secretary of UNPO (Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization). Ms Thinlay Chukki, Representative at the Tibet Bureau Geneva, has also spoken. * * * In the EU capital Brussels, a Prayer service was held for Lobga Rangzen at Nalanda Monastery, which was followed by a peace march at the Place de l’Albertine – the showcase square created for the Universal Exposition held in Brussels in 1910 – organised by the Regional Tibetan Youth Congress (RTYC), Belgium. * * * In Australia’s capital Canberra, The Office of Tibet of the CTA and the Australia Tibet Council (ATC) – led by Representative Karma Singey and ATC Executive Officer Dr Zoe Bedford – met with a bipartisan group of Australian lawmakers – including MPs Steve Georganas and Andrew Wallace and Senators Nick McKim and Steph Hodgins-May – to raise serious concerns over China’s new Ethnic Unity Law and its serious implications for Tibetans. They pointed out that activist Lobga Rangzen self-immolated a day after this law came into effect. As at numerous other protest locations, some 40 Tibetans – both men and women – clean-shaved their heads on the lawns of the Parliament House and in front of the Chinese Embassy to protest Beijing’s escalating foreign interference and honour a fallen activist, noted miragenews.com Aug 20. “The Prime Minister and Foreign Minister will be at the UN in New York next month, we expect them to raise Tibet,” Dr Zoȅ Bedford, Executive Officer of the Australia Tibet Council, has said. “This is cultural genocide carried out under a false banner of ethnic unity.” The report said approximately 300 Tibetan community members from Sydney, Canberra, Newcastle, Campbelltown, Blue Mountains and the South Coast (Nowra) travelled to Canberra to send a direct message to the Federal Government. Members of the Uyghur, Mongolian and pro-democracy Chinese communities have joined many of those events to express their solidarity with the Tibetan people and in recognition of the sacrifice of martyr Lobsang Palden.

title: Facts on Record: The Second Fact-Finding Delegation, 1980
author: tibetanreview
content: OPINION After witnessing a video commentary on the second fact-finding delegation sent by His Holiness the Dalai Lama which toured Tibet from 1 May 1980, Phuntsog Wangyal*, a member of that delegation, asks that the record be set straight on what he says are a number of factual errors in that commentary. Recently, a friend sent me a video (attached here) in which a person was giving a commentary about the delegation and its visit to Tibet. As I listened to it, I felt that the commentary had either been prepared in great haste or that the commentator had not had the opportunity to research and understand the subject fully. I noticed a number of factual errors and felt that it was important, as someone who was actually a member of the delegation, to put some of the facts on record. According to the commentator, we allegedly said to Ngapo ‘Ape’ Ngawang Jigme, “You sold Tibet in Chamdo; why didn’t you fight against the Chinese? etc.” I have no recollection whatsoever of such a statement being made by any of us. What I do remember clearly is that we spoke openly and frankly with Tibetans, even in the presence of Chinese officers and local Tibetan and Chinese officials. We did not hesitate to speak about what we had seen and learned on the ground. Our conversations were straightforward, open, and confident. We were there to see the situation for ourselves. Similarly, the commentator’s explanation of the visit being cut short by fifteen days is too simplified and, in my view, potentially misleading. The circumstances surrounding the shortening of the delegation’s visit had much more to do with the political situation at the time than his account suggests. The Second Tibetan Delegation, led by Tenzin Namgyal Tethong and his deputy Tsering Dorjee, with the Panchen Rinpoche in Beijing. The other members were Gyari Pema Gyalpo, Losang Jinpa and myself. To understand what actually happened, it is important to look at the circumstances in which the decision was made and to consider the contemporary reports rather than relying on a simplified account given many years later. The political sensitivities surrounding the delegation’s visit, our meetings with Tibetans, and what was being discussed and reported at the time all form part of the story. The Second Delegation was not simply a group of tourists following a predetermined itinerary. Its visit took place in a highly sensitive political environment, and what we saw, what Tibetans told us, and the discussions that took place inevitably had political implications. The Chinese authorities were also closely involved in the arrangements and were aware of what was taking place. For that reason, I believe that saying simply that the visit was “cut short by fifteen days” without explaining the circumstances gives an incomplete picture, potentially misleading. The reasons behind the decision are important for anyone trying to understand what happened during the delegation’s visit and the political atmosphere surrounding it. There are contemporary reports and records available which provide a much clearer picture of these events. They should be consulted before drawing conclusions about why the visit ended earlier than originally planned. For me, as someone who was a member of the delegation, it is important that this part of the history is also recorded accurately and in its proper political context. For those who would like to know more about what I personally witnessed and reported at the time, there is a contemporary record that may be of interest. I gave a personal report at a public meeting in Darjeeling in 1980. The meeting was recorded, and my report was subsequently published in the Tibetan-language newspaper Tibetan Freedom Press (བོད་མིའི་རང་དབང་།) on 19 September 1980. A similar report was also published in English in Tibet News Review, Vol. 1, Nos. 3/4, Winter 1980/81, published by the Tibetan Community in Britain. These contemporary records are important because they provide an account of the events written and published at the time, rather than many years later through the interpretation of others. I hope this helps provide a clearer understanding of the facts. — Phuntsog Wangyal* is a former Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in London and a former Member of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile

title: Latest satellite images confirm China’s continuing assault on Larung Gar Buddhist learning centre in Tibet
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug20’26) – Latest satellite images are stated to confirm reports that China has been carrying out large-scale demolitions at the famed – and the world’s largest Buddhist learning centre – located in a Tibetan County and prefecture in Sichuan Province. This has come as China began implementing its so-called Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law in its latest forced assimilation move that targets ethnic minorities and their cultural roots. Such demolitions have especially meant the expulsion of large numbers of various categories of students – monks, nuns and lay students and practitioners from other parts of the PRC as well as from other countries. Citing satellite imagery analyzed by Radio Free Asia (RFA), rfa.org said Aug 18 that Chinese authorities had over the past month continued and expanded demolition at the Larung Gar Buddhist Academy, located in Serthar County of Kardze Prefecture, which at its peak in the early 2000s was stated to be home to 40,000 Buddhist monastics. The report said the demolitions followed reports of new expulsion of thousands of Tibetan monks and nuns from the centre last year. The demolitions have been carried out at different phases since 2001 and this time, at least 1,060 residences belonging to monks and nuns are targeted for demolition, starting from around Jul 13, the report said, citing Tenzin Pema, director of strategic communication at the Washington-based International Campaign for Tibet (ICT), and formerly RFA Tibetan director. “RFA’s Aug 14 imagery appears to show clearance spreading around the academy’s central area, supporting our Jul 17 report that a new demolition campaign began around Jul 13,” Tenzin Pema has said. “The current campaign raises fears of another major assault on Tibetan Buddhist religious, cultural, and educational life.” The report said that satellite imagery captured on Aug 14 confirms that approximately 2.5 acres (1 hectare) had been cleared from a residential area of the academy since the demolition started. Dump trucks and excavators remain visible at the site, and demolition is scheduled to be completed by Aug 20, the report cited sources familiar with the situation on the ground in Serthar as saying. Comparing satellite images from July 24 and August 14 shows that the demolition zone has widened, with some sections now cleared of debris. Dump trucks and excavators remain active across the roughly 2.5‑acre (1‑hectare) site. (Image courtesy: RFA) Larung Gar is now about half of what it was at its peak after the expulsions and demolitions that have been carried out over the years. This included the expulsion of about 5,000 monks and nuns and the demolition of nearly 5,000 dwellings. Unlike in past years, this year’s demolitions were stated to include residences of monks and nuns who did not receive any prior public notice. Besides, current plans are stated to include the continuation of the demolish of additional residences next year. Tight restrictions on visitor In order to curtail information about the expulsions, demolitions, and intrusive administrative restrictions on the learning centre from reaching the outside world, the authorities are stated to have restricted visitors. The report said Serthar County Public Security Bureau had been reminding tourists that they must only travel to Larung Gar via official arrangements and were prohibited from entering on their own. Authorities have also warned visitors not to trust information provided by people with no connection to the local area and prohibited individuals from bypassing restricted areas or crossing mountains to enter the site independently. Visitors are said to be allowed to remain for no more than 90 minutes and must travel in designated shuttle buses. They are also required to rent a small electronic tracking device for 200 yuan ($29). The device is stated to be used to monitor visitors’ movements, enforce time limits and restrict access to certain areas. Telephone conversations with individuals in and around Larung Gar are believed to be closely monitored by Chinese security authorities, making residents reluctant to speak openly. Local people are seen to be increasingly afraid to answer questions directly about conditions at Larung Gar. In fact, this level of surveillance is no longer unique to the area but has become common across many parts of Tibet, the report said. Established in 1980 with support from the late 10th Panchen Lama to revive Buddhist scholarship in the aftermath of the devastation wrought by the decade-long Cultural Revolution (!966-76), Larung Gar grew into what may have been the world’s largest centre for Tibetan Buddhist learning. Over the decades, it became one of the most influential centres for the study of Tibetan language, culture, and religion, attracting thousands of Chinese Buddhist practitioners, in addition to Tibetans.

title: China-appointed Panchen has asserted that ‘true Dharma’ begins with observing the coercive ethic unity law
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug20’26) – While members of China’s so-called ethnic Minority groups in the free world, including Tibetans, as well as the international community, have condemned China’s recently implemented Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law as a tool of forced assimilation, the Chinese government-installed “11 th Panchen Lama” Gyaltsen Norbu has on Aug 14 called the law a powerful instrument of national law and also an embodiment of the true Dharma on which religious precepts should be based, according to China’s online Tibet news service eng.tibet.cn Aug 18. Ethnic unity is the foundation of national unity, the cornerstone of social harmony, and the source of development and progress. The law offers robust institutional safeguards for strengthening the sense of community for the Chinese nation and consolidating the foundations of ethnic unity, and serves as a fundamental measure to consolidate and advance the cause of ethnic unity and progress in the new era, he has said. Addressing a symposium in Lhasa for representatives of non-CPC (Communist Party of China) individuals in Xizang (Tibet Autonomous Region) to study, publicize and implement the Ethnic Unity Law, Gyaltsen Norbu has asserted that national law takes precedence over religious precepts, and believing in the true Dharma must begin with observing discipline and the law. He has vowed to devote himself to studying the essence of the law, embrace its spirit, follow the principles of upholding the law, and guide monks, nuns and followers in Tibetan Buddhism to understand that the law is a strong legal safeguard protecting their lawful rights and interests and an important standard for handling ethnic affairs in the new era. He was stated to have maintained that building a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation was highly consistent with the fine Buddhist tradition of solemnizing the land and bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. According to him, building a shared spiritual home depends above all on a shared cultural identity, with patriotism as its foundation. “The motherland is the place where we are born, raised and nurtured, and to which our deepest emotions belong. Loving the country and loving one’s religion has never been an empty slogan; it is a responsibility that every Buddhist disciple should fulfil.” To “keep the fundamental interests of the country in mind” means embracing the shared symbols and image of China and repaying the great kindness of the Communist Party of China and the land that has nurtured us. “Only by loving and serving the country can we fulfil the Buddhist aspiration for a prosperous and peaceful age,” he has asserted. Basing himself on President Xi Jinping’s “new era” slogan, Gylatsen Norbu has said that those who observe religious precepts should take “safeguarding ethnic unity” as a solemn personal responsibility and put the principle of unity of “body, speech and mind” into practice from the depths of their hearts. He has called on monks, nuns and Buddhist followers “to study and understand the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law in accordance with its principles, set aside prejudice and division, reach a common understanding and firmly develop a law-based mindset,” so that “the law can better fulfil its purpose and bring greater benefits to all.” Noting that religious figures occupy a unique position that enables them to connect with the broader community of religious believers, Gylatsen Norbu has said, “Under the guidance of the CPC and the government, we will lead by example and actively create opportunities and platforms for exchanges, interaction and integration among all ethnic groups through religious activities, cultural exchanges, public welfare and charitable initiatives, and other areas. We should guide monks, nuns and Buddhist followers to respect, study, observe and apply the law.’ Calling on people to “remain firm and unwavering in safeguarding national unity and clearly oppose separatism,” the China-installed “11 th Panchen Lama” has said, “The Tibetan Buddhist community should regard the implementation of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law as an opportunity in keeping with Buddhist principles and the needs of the times, and repay the kindness of the country through concrete action.” “I will take this law as a guiding light and contribute the wisdom and strength that the religious community can offer to the development of a modern socialist Xizang and the great cause of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation,” he was quoted as saying, using the Sinicized name for Tibet Autonomous Region.

title: Xi Jinping praises Tiananmen crackdown on Jiang Zemin’s birth centenary, paints a bright future for China under his leadership
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Aug20’26) – While even an indication of referring to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre by ordinary citizens invites instant merciless crackdown, President Xi Jinping has on Aug 17 praised the Communist Party of China (CPC) he heads for that clampdown in a landmark speech marking the centenary of the birth of one of his predecessors – Jiang Zemin – who rose to power in its aftermath. Jiang was China’s top party leader from 1989 to 2002, state president from 1993 to 2003, and continued as the chairman of the Central Military Commission from 1989 to 2004. He died in 2022. It was a bullish speech in which Xi, Addressing thousands of officials and delegates in the Great Hall of the People, called on his country to show an “indomitable fighting spirit”, noted edition.cnn.com Aug 17. In his 45-minute speech, Xi praised a long list of Jiang’s achievements, including a rare mention of the Tiananmen square democracy protests, hailing the CPC’s ultimate decision to reject the protesters’ demands and clear the square using troops and tanks, calling the student-led democracy protest that began in Apr 1989 “a serious political upheaval”. “In between of the spring and summer of 1989, China experienced a serious political upheaval, Comrade Jiang Zemin resolutely supported and implemented the Central Committee’s correct decisions, effectively maintaining stability in Shanghai,” Xi was quoted as saying. The protest began after widespread mourning for the death on Apr 15, 1989 of Hu Yaobang, who was seen by the public as a champion for liberalization and who had been ousted from his position two years earlier. Days after Hu’s death, thousands of grieving students marched through Beijing, calling for a more democratic government in his honour. Protesters gathered on Tiananmen Square and their numbers continued to swell over several weeks until Jun 4, when the People’s Liberation Army troops of the CPC sent in tanks and fired on them. The role played by the then President Yang Shangkun during the protest was stated to have caused a fundamental shift in China’s political structure. Yang was at first sympathetic to the students and sided with General Secretary Zhao Ziyang in supporting them. As the Vice Chairman and Secretary-General of the Central Military commission, he even praised Zhao’s position by claiming that his “notion of pacifying the student movement through democracy and law is good and seems quite workable right now.” However, Zhao’s position was stated to have been contested by Premier Li Peng and Party elder Li Xianniuan, who wanted to use force to suppress the student demonstrations and reportedly engaged in an internal power struggle with Zhao to convince other senior leaders of their position. After the hardliners gained the upper hand with then paramount leader Deng Xiaoping’s support, Yang was stated to have changed his position and supported the use of force to suppress student protestors. In May 1989, he appeared on state television, where he denounced the student demonstrations as “anarchy” and defended the imposition of martial law on several areas of Beijing affected by the protests. Jiang unexpectedly became General Secretary of the CPC shortly after the crackdown in part because the person he replaced, Zhao Ziyang, was seen as being unduly sympathetic to the protesters. By 1993 Jiang was the undisputed leader of China, the report noted. Jiang’s contribution to support party rulers’ decision to clamp down on protesters was also stated to have been mentioned in a 12-episode documentary that aired on state TV last week to commemorate his life. However, it did not show any footage of the killings that shocked the world. Those images are routinely scrubbed from China’s heavily censored internet and discussion of what happened remains fraught with risk to this day, the report said. Jiang’s term saw China’s economy charge ahead and open up to the world, culminating in the country joining the World Trade Organization – with US support – in 2001. It was a period of intense economic growth for China, with improved relations with the US. In his speech, which was also broadcast and published by state media, Xi has talked up the nation’s accomplishments under his leadership, saying that “people’s lives continue to improve,” even as data shows slowing economic growth, the report noted. “The prospects for the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation are bright, and the dream for which several generations have strived with unwavering determination is gradually becoming a reality,” he has added.

title: Witnesses estimate deaths, missing in Tibet due to Aug 26 Nepal-border flash floods to be much higher
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep08’26) – While China has said nothing about any devastation caused on towns, villages and other human settlements in Kyirong County in Tibet as a result of the catastrophic flash floods of ice, rock, mud, and, of course, water in the morning of Aug 26, the Tibetan Service of Radio Free Asia ( rfa.org ) reported Sep 6, citing a local Tibetan source, that 26 people had lost their lives in one village alone. However, the report did not say whether other villages and so forth were also hit by the flash flood. China has officially confirmed that as of Sep 5, a total of 43 people had died on the Tibet side, with 519 people missing, including 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries. The report cited the Tibetan resident as saying 26 people had died in Risur village, where the Gyirong Port is located. The report also cited a Chinese resident from Kyirong Port, who wasn’t at the border crossing when the mudslide struck, as saying “No one at the border checkpoint appears to have survived,” adding about 800 people lived there. An official CGTN video report carried by the state news outlet chinadaily.com.cn Sep 8 said the Gyirong Port was one of the first populated areas to be hit by the flash flood on the Tibet side. It did not say which other populated areas were hit there. China’s official globaltimes.cn said Sep 7, citing CCTV News , that after hitting the Kyirong River, the high-speed flow of the debris of ice, rock, mud and water split in two directions, with one moving nearly 3 kilometres upstream and the other continuing downstream into Nepal for tens of kilometres. The CGTN video report said the flash flood hit Kyirong river at the speed of a bullet train, covering 22 km in just 7 minutes to destroy 27 buildings there. Meanwhile, the identities of some of the victims on the Tibet side have been confirmed. So far, none of the bodies retrieved are foreign nationals, reported China’s official Xinhua news agency Sep 8. The report cited Yang Lahong, deputy director of the foreign affairs office of Tibet Autonomous Region as saying at a briefing that the names and specific information of missing foreigners had not been made public to protect their privacy, but had been shared with the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels. The Indian Embassy in China on Sep 7 asked families of Indians missing since the Aug 26 flash flood to provide DNA samples to help identify them. The request came after Chinese authorities confirmed that they were now able to receive DNA samples from families of Indian nationals listed as missing in the disaster, indiatoday.in Sep 7 cited an Embassy press release as saying.

title: How not to be a human rights lawyer in China
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep08’26) – China’s new rules for becoming a lawyer is a cautionary tale on how not to become one especially if one’s main interest is to become a human rights lawyer. The Party-state has made support for the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leadership an explicit legal qualification for lawyers, said an organiser.org commentary Sep 3, citing an amendment to the country’s Lawyers Law, adopted by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress on Aug 28 and enacted on Sep 1. The amendment turned a political requirement previously imposed through Ministry of Justice regulations into a formal requirement of national law. The move effectively introduced a political loyalty test for lawyers before they can practise in China. The change gives the requirement of political loyalty to the CCP a stronger statutory foundation. The amendment not only requires applicants to support China’s Constitution but also “the leadership of the Communist Party of China” and the country’s “socialist rule of law.” The previous previous requirements stated that prospective lawyers should support the Constitution, pass the national legal qualification examination, complete a one-year internship and demonstrate good character. So, becoming a lawyer is no longer framed only around professional qualifications and legal competence but explicit political loyalty to the CCP leadership. This means that for rights activist lawyers and legal professionals handling politically sensitive cases, the change further narrows the space for independent legal practice. The new requirements are pretty stringent. The amended law introduces a new Article 3, stating that lawyers must adhere to CCP leadership and implement the policies and decisions of the Party and the state. The provision places Communist leadership directly within the statutory framework governing legal practice in China, the commentary noted. The rules have already required law firms with three or more CCP members to establish Communist Party organisations. Firms with fewer CCP members were required to conduct Party work through joint organisations or Party-building instructors. Law firms have been further required to create mechanisms to allow Party organisations to participate in decision-making and management, while providing space, personnel and funding for Party activities. The Aug 28 amendment moves all these requirements into national legislation. The law’s guarantees of protecting “lawyers’ lawful practice”, and the requirement for courts, prosecutors, police, state-security agencies and judicial-administration departments to establish systems protecting lawyers’ professional right are, therefore, subject to the overriding requirement of fealty to the governing CCP regime. The changes in the rules and now the law followed the so-called “709 Crackdown” which began on Jul 9, 2015 under which more than 300 lawyers, legal assistants and rights advocates were detained, questioned or otherwise swept up. Some lawyers were held incommunicado or subsequently prosecuted on national-security charges, while others lost their law licences. The pressure also extended to their families. Spouses and children reported surveillance, movement restrictions, pressure on landlords and interference with schooling, the commentary noted. Wang Yu, a rights lawyer detained during the “709 Crackdown”, has described her assessment of China’s legal system in an interview in Jun 2018: “Now I believe there is no law in China.” She argued that the essence of the rule of law is limiting government power, while the CCP was using the rule of law to reinforce its own rule, the commentary said.

title: The Dilemma of the Democratic System of the Tibetan Government-in-Exile
author: tibetanreview
content: Prof. Thomas Kell* dissects the exile Tibetan democracy, examines its fundamental shortcomings, practical dilemmas. and hidden dangers, and wonders whether the existing structure can independently maintain political continuity and the legitimacy of the movement in the post-Dalai Lama scenario without adequately adapting the institutional design to the realities of a shrinking, dispersed exile population and the generational change. As a researcher in Tibetan studies, I have interviewed many Tibetans in exile, including former Sikyong Lobsang Sangay, and heard numerous views on the “democratic system” of the Tibetan government-in-exile (referred to as Central Tibetan Administration, or CTA). In my opinion, the democratic system of the Tibetan government-in-exile suffers from multiple structural defects and practical dilemmas. The following represents only my personal views and is offered for discussion. The democratic system of the Tibetan government-in-exile began in the 1960s. The Charter of the Tibetans-in-Exile of 1991 established a three-branch framework, and after the Dalai Lama formally transferred political power in 2011, it was further “democratized,” with the election of a Sikyong (political leader) and a parliament. However, it is not the democracy of a mature sovereign state, but a limited experiment of a refugee community in exile. Its problems are particularly evident in inadequate representation, institutional fragility, the entanglement of religion and politics, and low governance effectiveness. I. Lack of a sovereign foundation: democracy remains largely formal The CTA has no territory, no army, and no coercive enforcement powers; it operates entirely under the legal frameworks of host countries such as India. Its “judicial institution” (the Tibetan Supreme Justice Commission) is in essence closer to an arbitration body and cannot exercise genuine judicial independence or coercive authority. Voter eligibility depends on registration through the “Green Book,” and voting is dispersed across settlements and diaspora communities worldwide. Participation is severely constrained by geography, resources, and the policies of host countries. This “stateless democracy” makes the system inherently fragile: its budget relies on diaspora donations and external aid (for example, U.S. assistance has faced the risk of being frozen), and its core functions focus on refugee services and cultural preservation rather than effective political decision-making. Should the attitude of a host country change or aid diminish, the entire system faces an operational crisis. II. Clear unfairness and distortions in the electoral and representational mechanisms The parliament has 45 seats and uses a mixed model based on the three traditional regions (U-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo) with 10 seats each (including women’s quotas) + 10 seats for religious schools (Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, Gelug, and Bön) + a limited number of seats for overseas Tibetans, rather than pure one-person-one-vote or allocation according to the current population. Tibetans overseas (especially those outside South Asia) have very few seats, creating a de facto hierarchy of citizenship rights. The allocation of religious representatives directly grants the monastic community disproportionate political weight, contradicting the principle of equality proclaimed in the Charter and reinforcing residual theocratic elements. In addition, electoral rules restrict regional associations, religious schools, and NGOs from openly nominating or campaigning for candidates, effectively suppressing the development of party politics. Although there is democracy in name, there is a lack of mature opposition parties and competition based on programmatic platforms. Elections often devolve into contests of personal image and negative mudslinging. The limited and dispersed voter base, further subject to external interference (such as voting being obstructed in parts of Nepal), further undermines the fairness and credibility of the process. III. Repeated institutional deadlock and excessive reliance on personal authority After 2011, although the Dalai Lama withdrew from politics, his moral and spiritual influence continues to dominate. In 2021, the parliament’s impeachment of the justice commissioners triggered a constitutional crisis: the newly elected parliament could not be sworn in, the Sikyong could not form a cabinet, and the budget could not be approved. The stalemate lasted for months and was ultimately resolved only through the Dalai Lama’s intervention. Since then, the parliament has repeatedly adjourned or postponed sessions due to walkouts and lack of quorum, while judicial positions have remained vacant for long periods because of qualification requirements that are difficult to meet. These crises expose the failure of checks and balances: the boundaries between the legislative, executive, and judicial branches are blurred, and effective conflict-resolution mechanisms are lacking. In the exile environment, the logic of “unity first” is inherently in conflict with the pluralism and competition required by democracy, leading to intensified polarization and deepening rifts within the community. Divisions based on regional identity, religious background, and the “Middle Way” versus independence lines frequently turn into parliamentary internal strife rather than policy debate. IV. Incomplete disentanglement of religion and politics limits the quality of democracy Although secularized in form, the Charter still retains the concept of the “coexistence of religion and politics.” Religious representative seats, the influence of monastics in the community, and residual elements of historical familial and theocratic politics make it difficult for the system to fully escape the shadow of traditional theocracy. The Dalai Lama’s personal authority remains the ultimate arbiter at critical moments, indicating that the democratic system has not yet achieved genuine self-sustainability and secularization. At the same time, the absence of genuine multi-party competition and open public debate means that public opinion and organizational activities are constrained by internal community pressures, making it difficult to achieve adequate supervision and accountability. V. Insufficient governance effectiveness and long-term sustainability The CTA’s administrative focus has long remained on settlement services and cultural maintenance, with limited substantive impact on the situation inside Tibet. Internal polarization, crises of trust after leadership transitions, and a sense of alienation among the younger generation are all weakening cohesion. Facing the Dalai Lama’s advanced age and the uncertainties surrounding the question of reincarnation, whether the existing democratic structure can independently maintain political continuity and the legitimacy of the movement remains a major hidden danger. The institutional design has not adequately adapted to the realities of a shrinking, dispersed exile population and generational change. — * Thomas Kell, a Professor at Georgetown University Law Center, primarily focuses his research on the application of international law to geopolitical disputes in South Asia. Influenced by this work, he also developed a particular interest in Tibet and the Tibetan government-in-exile. After recently reading the statement issued by the Tibetan government-in-exile on the 66th Tibetan Democracy Day, he seeks to discuss with the Tibetan exile community, from a legal perspective, the shortcomings existing in the Tibetan democratic system.

title: China suppressing information, silencing victims, even as it takes a foreign media group to flood-ravaged Kyirong
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep06’26) – As families of pilgrims visiting Tibet from abroad who went missing after the devastating flash floods of ice, rock, and mud on Aug 26 morning demand answers on what was being done to find out about their fate or whereabouts, China has, for the first time, opened Gyirong (Tibetan: Kyirong) County in Tibet to a select group of foreign journalists, including the CNN and PTI , on Sep 6 . However, it is a carefully arranged visit in an effort to show the rescue operations going on at the Gyirong Port, said edition.cnn.com Sep 6. The visit to Kyirong County – which was jointly organized by China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and State Council Information Office, with the itinerary planned by the officials to access this restricted area – was aimed only at showing the destruction caused by the floods and the relief and reconstruction work now under way, said the PTI report Sep 6. China’s official Xinhua news agency said Sep 6 that the number of the dead in the Kyirong border area now stood at 43 as of Sep 6 at 6pm, with 519 missing. It did not say how many of either of these two figures include foreigners. It previously said the missing figure included 261 foreigners from 23 countries. China claims transparency and cooperation with other countries, but diplomats report no clear plan for DNA identification or sharing of vital data like video or facial recognition, reported Reuters Sep 5. The report said families accuse China of an information blackout, with no updates on missing persons or victim identification efforts, increasing their frustration and uncertainty. “There is no update from China about what is happening at Ground Zero, what is the situation over there,” Tarun, brother of a missing pilgrim has said. His sister, Priyanka Choudhary, an Indian-born Finnish citizen, was returning from a Hindu pilgrimage in Tibet, and was at a border crossing with Nepal when a catastrophic mudslide hit, the report said. Likewise, Naresh Goyal, brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, a 51-year-old British national, has said, “We are not getting anything from China, whether my sister is safe or alive or dead.” The report said China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the accusations, the timeline for victim identification, or DNA collection protocols being used on the Tibetan side. In Nepal, authorities, including the police, regularly share information on those missing and dead on social media, while search efforts have been accompanied by active DNA testing, the report noted. In addition, China has not offered to provide video from its side of the land port, including facial-recognition images, that could be shared with families or used in identifying the dead, the report cited diplomats in contact with China’s foreign ministry as saying. * * * Chinese authorities said they have been rebuilding roads to restore access to the cut-off border post and have also sent relief materials to Nepal. The journalists’ visit to Kyirong County was aimed at showing both the destruction caused by the floods and the relief and reconstruction work now under way, said the PTI report. Likewise, the CNN report said, “Information about who was impacted here has been slow to emerge from the port, cutting a contrast with Nepal where there have been frequent updates on the numbers of rescued or confirmed dead.” Chinese authorities have yet to publicly release a list of names of those who were at the port at the time or who are believed to be missing on this side of the border. That’s prompted questions about transparency – especially from families who are desperate for news of missing loved ones, the report said. The report continued, “Beijing has defended its release of information from its remote disaster area as open and timely. Its invitation to a group of around a dozen reporters from international news outlets – including CNN – for Sunday’s carefully arranged visit to the area is part of an effort to show the rescue operations going on at the port.” “We’re mainly focused on intensive search and rescue operations at this stage,” Zhang, who had been working at the site since access opened on Sep 2, has said. “Our approach is to dig one layer, search that layer, and then clear it before moving on to the next. We’re digging very carefully, searching thoroughly and clearing the debris layer by layer to see if we can find any of the deceased.” But there is still total lack of information on how the disaster hit the local area on the Tibetan side of the border on Aug 26 morning and its effects on people, their homes and families. Human Rights Watch said some Chinese journalists had been instructed not to interview relatives of people killed or missing and to rely only on material provided by Xinhua , noted the timesofindia.com Sep 5.

title: Human-induced heating, including climbers’ urinating, contributing to rapid melting of Himalayan glaciers
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep05’26) – China and Nepal may have to seriously consider curtailing or, otherwise, better managing their Mt Everest economy if they are to slow the pace of the already rapidly melting glaciers around the world’s tallest peak under the effects of global warming, according to a recent study. On the Nepali side, the quest to conquer Mt Everest is melting the Khumbu glacier on top of which a base camp is set up every season. The study has shown that human activities here, including urination, are melting this glacier rapidly, with the ground temperature rising every year, reported wionews.com Sep 4, citing the study. On the Tibetan side, the North Everest Base Camp is set up near the historic Rongbuk Monastery at an altitude of about 5,150 to 5,200 meters (16,900 feet) every climbing season. It is not clear whether there has been a similar study on that side of Mt Everest. The study on the Khumbu glacier base camp, published by a group of Nepali and American scientists in the journal Regional Environmental Change, shows how this human activity is driving the glacier to melt, setting the stage for an imminent disaster, the report said. Image courtesy: Google Earth/BBC It was stated to be a glacial lake outburst which shook the Kyirong-Rasuwa, Tibet-Nepal border port crossing with a massive flash flood on Aug 26, 2026 morning, washing away villages and marketplaces, and killing, potential, thousands of people. Information on the disaster on the Tibetan side of the border has been severely restricted or curtailed by China, with nothing available about victims and damages, but just numbers of the officially reported dead and missing, and a great deal about how the authorities are coping with the aftermath of the disaster. The new study is stated to focus on how, along with global warming and fossil fuel consumption, human urinary discharge is also causing the glacier to melt. The higher altitude requires climbers to drink more water, in turn leading them to pee more. According to the researchers, in the 2023 season, nearly 6,766 litres of urine were produced per day. Khim Lal Gautam and his colleagues have said that urine alone carries a lot of heat and is enough to cause considerable melting of the glacier, although it is far from being the main contributing factor. Estimating how much ice that amount of heat could melt, the researchers have said the glacier lost 154 tons of ice in that climbing season alone. However, human urine is not the biggest factor. After exiting the body at around 37 degrees Celsius, it cools down as well. Researchers have calculated how much ice it could melt in this state. And they have noted that only a little of that heat reaches the ice, as the rest either escapes into the air or rocks. The bigger problem has been found to be all the fuel consumption linked to the Base Camp. In the 2023 season alone, 824 cylinders of LPG, 18,935 litres of kerosene and 5,130 litres of gasoline were used for cooking, heating and electricity. It accounted for about 94 per cent of the melting caused by humans, while urine made up the other 6 per cent, the study has found. Scientists have been warning that the Himalayas are warming faster than other regions. Ice loss nearly doubled after 2000, compared to the previous quarter, as per a 2019 study published in Science Advances . The team has said that the surface temperatures at Base Camp are increasing faster than other parts of the Khumbu Glacier, rising at about 0.28 degrees Celsius per year. The scientists have called for better waste management and reliance on solar power.

title: Global press watchdog condemns China’s Tibet-blackout on Aug 26 flash flood crisis
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep05’26) – One of the world’s top press freedom organisations has on Sep 2 strongly condemned China for imposing sweeping restrictions on media professionals from accessing vital information on the Tibetan side of the border following the devastating glacier-avalanche triggered Tibet-Nepal flash floods of Aug 26 morning. Expressing grave concern, Paris-based Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said that no independent Tibetan media outlet or international news organisation had been granted access to the disaster-stricken Kyirong area of Tibet. This “reflects a long-standing practice of the Chinese regime, which exercises some of the strictest control in the world over media professionals,” the group said. In its report, titled as Floods in Nepal and Tibet: restrictions and disinformation are impeding vital news , the group noted that the Chinese authorities had only authorised state media to cover the floods in Tibetan areas, with reports highlighting Beijing’s achievements and successes in relief efforts rather than providing a comprehensive account of the scale and impact of the devastation. Tibet has become a “de facto information black hole” in recent years under Chinese President Xi Jinping’s leadership, Aleksandra Bielakowska, Head of Advocacy, RSF Asia-Pacific, has said. “No independent Tibetan media, nor any international media, are permitted to freely cover news from this autonomous region. The only outlets allowed to operate are those controlled by the state and its propaganda organs, which report on events in accordance with the guidelines approved by the Chinese Communist Party’s Propaganda Department. Under these circumstances, it is virtually impossible to gauge the true scale of the tragedy, as the regime seeks to whitewash its international image and stifle any information that might cast it in an unfavourable light,” Bielakowska has stated. “I noticed a very high level of censorship and information control inside Tibet. I also tried to reach Tibetans in exile whose families are in the flood-affected areas. Many have been reluctant to share information because they fear that speaking publicly could put their families inside Tibet at risk,” Kalsang Jigme, editor-in-chief of the independent media outlet Tibet Radio, has told RSF. Tibet Radio has said it independently confirmed the Tibetan death toll in Kyirong was at least 29 at a time when Chinese state media cited 16 deaths. RSF has also highlighted widespread censorship on Chinese social media, particularly on the platform WeChat , where references to the floods have been censored or deleted by the authorities. It cited Chinese state media to note that at least 10 internet users had been punished for allegedly “spreading rumours” related to the disaster. While the glacier-avalanche may have occurred on the Nepali side of the border, the flash flood it triggered first hit the Kyirong County’s border in Chinese ruled Tibet.

title: Dalai Lama back in D’shala after over two months in Ladakh
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep04’26) – The Dalai Lama returned to his exile home in Dharamshala, India, on Sep 4 morning to a rousing yet solemn welcome by the Tibetan and local host community after a knee surgery in Delhi followed by over two month’s summer stay in Ladakh, during which he gave audiences to more than 21,500 devotees, said the Central Tibetan Administration on its Tibet.net website Sep 4. While in Ladakh, the Dalai Lama attended celebrations marking his 91 st birthday on the Kalachakra Teaching Ground in capital Leh, located near his Shewatsel residence. He also attended prayer ceremonies at the Buddha statue in Stok and at the Buddha statue and stupa in Gonpa Village, besides visiting the Buddha Garden at the Mahabodhi International Meditation Centre. The Dalai Lama also attended the final session of the Yarchos Chenmo (Great Summer Debate) at the Matho Teaching Ground, as well as a long-life prayer offering on the Kalachakra Teaching Ground. The latter event, attended by more than 15,000 devotees, was jointly organised by the Ladakh Buddhist Association, Ladakh Gonpa Association, and the Tibetan Community in Ladakh. He topped his Ladakh stay by attending a thanksgiving and farewell cultural programme on the Kalachakra Teaching Ground on Sep 1, organized by the above groups and the Union Territory’s Muslim community. All in all, the Dalai Lama gave audiences to a total of 21,572 devotees. The Dalai Lama initially travelled to Delhi where he underwent surgery on his left knee on Jun 8, having previously had surgery on his right knee in Jun 2024 in New York City. He then flew to Ladakh on Jun 28 where he has spent much of his summer months in past many years. A widely anticipated meeting in Ladakh with the visiting US ambassador to India, Mr Sergio Gor, who is known to be close to President Donald Trump, eventually did not materialise. Gor was in Ladakh over Aug 20-21.

title: China warns of more Tibet glacier collapses, disasters after the deadly Aug 26 floods
author: tibetanreview
content: (TibetanReview.net, Sep04’26) – Referring to the devastating glacier-avalanche triggered Tibet-Nepal flash floods of Aug 26 morning that wiped out villages and markets while claiming what may amount to several thousand lives, China said Sep 2 that such disasters may become more frequent as a result of global warming. Many will argue that China’s infrastructure, mining, and resettlement devastation of the Himalayan environment plays big role in this worsening situation. Glacier disasters could become more frequent as global warming further weakens glacier stability on the Tibetan Plateau (now being referred to by China as “Qinghai-Xizang” Plateau after previously calling it “Qinghai-Tibet” Plateau), potentially triggering cascading effects that amplify damage and widen their impact, reported China’s Party mouthpiece globaltimes.cn Sep 2, citing an announcement that day by the country’s National Climate Centre. After analyzing remote-sensing monitoring data and information transmitted from the Tibet-Nepal disaster site, and combining these findings with on-site inspections and field visits, the cryosphere emergency response and disaster mitigation team of the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, concluded that at around 10:52 am on Aug 26, a glacier on the northern slope of Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal broke off at an elevation of approximately 5,200 metres, triggering an ice-and-rock avalanche, the report said. After explaining how the Aug 26 disaster played out, giving no room for immediate counteraction, the report cited Gao Rong, deputy director of China’s National Climate Centre, as saying during a press conference held by the China Meteorological Administration on Sep 2 that global warming is accelerating the melting of mountain glaciers worldwide. Climate warming has altered the dynamic characteristics of glaciers, leading to rising ice temperatures, faster glacier flow and more frequent surges. Since the beginning of the 21st century, particularly since 2010, ice avalanche events in high-altitude mountainous regions around the world have been on the rise. Against the backdrop of a warmer and wetter climate on the Tibetan Plateau, glaciers across the region are generally undergoing accelerated melting, Gao has said. SOURCE Google Earth Citing the Glacier Inventory of what constitutes the People’s Republic of China, Gao has said that glacier coverage on the Tibetan Plateau has shrunk by about 24 percent over the past 60 years, with some 7,000 small glaciers disappearing entirely. Rapid warming on the Tibetan Plateau is driving accelerated melting of the cryosphere, leading to an increase in the number of glacial lakes and rapid expansion of their area, while glaciers are becoming dynamically unstable, Gao has added. The cryosphere is the frozen water part of the Earth system, covering all regions where water exists in solid form like ice, snow, and permafrost. It is expected that the internal structural stability of glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau will decline further in the future.
